#5742. HealthTap unveils virtual primary care program for Medicare Advantage plans

HealthTap unveils virtual primary care program for Medicare Advantage plans" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

HealthTap is rolling out a new program for Medicare Advantage plans that seeks to help members form a connection with a primary care doctor that carries forward.

The program leans on a combination of proactive outreach and access to a patient's historical medical records to support plans in identifying needs or risks, filling care gaps and coordinating follow-up or other necessary care. It's built to directly support individuals who may not have a PCP on file.

HealthTap reaches out to those members proactively, the company said, and helps them schedule an initial virtual visit with a provider who stays connected for preventive services, chronic condition management and medication concerns.

"The angle that we're taking is: wouldn't it be cool if, in fact, your virtual primary care physician was just like a bricks and mortar primary care physician?" said Rick Cochran, senior vice president of health plans at HealthTap, in an interview with Fierce Healthcare.

In an ideal scenario, a patient who has a consistent primary care physician who they see over the course of multiple years and who they come to trust, he said. HealthTap is looking to build that experience with virtual primary care docs, and reach patients who are disconnected from the health system with critical services.

Cochran said that the team, at times, receives feedback about concern that a program like this could upset in-network practices. However, he said that HealthTap views these service lines as complementary, and the company as offering another way for insurers to reach members who are underserved and in need of help.

"There's a bunch of people who haven't been receiving care that we can work with," he said. "We're not attempting to disrupt anything. We're attempting to complement things."

Through the program, HealthTap can connect with members via text messaging, email, direct mail or phone, at the plan's discretion. The member can then schedule the appointment for themselves and choose a board-certified primary care physician based in their state.

Between video visits, the member can also connect with their physician through secure messaging, HealthTap said.

In aiming to make the experience feel as much like traditional, brick-and-mortar clinics as possible, Cochran said that members are allowed to switch their physicians and find the one that best matches their individual health needs.

And to better support the physicians, HealthTap pulls from health information networks to pull key medical records, including relevant data from before an individual enrolled in their current plan. That set-up also means that the patient can carry their relationship with a HealthTap doc forward should they switch plans, Cochran said.

Cochran said that COVID-19 really kicked down the door to virtual care for seniors, and there's significant opportunity in MA for a program like HealthTap's, as these patients often have multiple comorbidities and may face barriers to seeing a doctor in person, such as the lack of transportation.

The company did an initial deployment with one MA plan and found that 35% of the initial outreach cohort scheduled an appointment, and 19% completed their first visit within six weeks. Satisfaction scores for both patients and physicians are high, Cochran said.

The approach gives doctors more time to spend working "to make people better, not crank through visits," he said.

"Our physician satisfaction score is very high because our physicians have the time to spend with the patient to ensure that the patient's needs are met," he said.

#5741. Norway’s Electric Snowplow Worked. Sweden Added Hydrogen Anyway.

Norway has already demonstrated battery-electric snowplowing on one of its toughest mountain highways. A Scania 45 R covered roughly 7,000 km on Hardangervidda, plowing, grading and spreading sand through a Norwegian winter. Its performance exceeded expectations. Meanwhile, Sweden has unveiled a hydrogen snowplow that is, in fact, another large battery-electric truck, with a fuel cell and hydrogen tanks added for extra range. The engineering question is why that second energy system is worth having when batteries are already doing the work, and when a conventional generator running on renewable diesel could offer a simpler, potentially cheaper route to occasional extended operation.

The Swedish vehicle has to compete with more than diesel snowplows. My full TFIE Strategy Briefing examines Norway’s measured electric operation, China’s expanding snow-removal equipment market and the additional costs hydrogen must justify.

Sweden’s project brings together Scania, MaserFrakt and Peab. The vehicle carries a 356 kWh rechargeable battery and 56 kg of hydrogen. The fuel cell generates electricity to extend the truck’s operating time between charging sessions. That gives the vehicle two energy-storage systems, plus the equipment to convert hydrogen into electricity. It will still need electric charging, and it will also need hydrogen production, delivery, storage and refueling.

Norway’s experience makes the starting point uncomfortable for hydrogen advocates. The Norwegian Public Roads Administration’s 2025 trial demonstrated that a production-based heavy electric truck could do demanding winter-maintenance work. Its measured consumption averaged approximately 2.02 kWh/km, with around six and a half hours of operating endurance under evaluated mixed-duty conditions. The trial identified shortcomings in charging compatibility and payload, but these were engineering and operating problems to resolve, not evidence that battery-electric snowplows were incapable of doing the job.

China is moving toward broader deployment. Municipalities have used smaller electric snow-removal equipment for years, while manufacturers have developed full-sized specialized electric vehicles. Beijing’s Mentougou district awarded contracts for 24 multifunction snow-removal trucks in September 2026. The final chassis specifications have not all been confirmed as battery-electric, but the procurement demonstrates a market moving beyond isolated demonstrations.

China’s much larger battery-electric truck industry is also providing specialized equipment manufacturers with an expanding supply of powertrains, batteries and heavy-duty chassis. Electric snowplows benefit from components developed and manufactured for freight vehicles at much greater volumes.

The Swedish approach looks increasingly difficult to justify against that background. If six or seven hours of productive operation is adequate, a battery-electric truck can already do the work. If longer shifts are required, larger batteries, better charging arrangements, mobile charging equipment or operational changes deserve assessment first. Hydrogen cannot claim the extreme-duty market merely because charging requires planning.

There is another alternative that the hydrogen comparison tends to omit. A conventional generator running on hydrotreated vegetable oil, or HVO, could supply additional electricity when the battery needs support. Diesel generators, fuel tanks and liquid-fuel distribution systems are mature technologies. Major generator manufacturers already approve suitable equipment for HVO, which can use conventional diesel-type storage and handling systems. Integrating a generator into a particular electric truck still requires engineering, certification and emissions controls, but it avoids constructing a hydrogen supply chain for a small fleet of seasonal vehicles.

For some operators, the even easier solution is to retain existing diesel snow-removal equipment and use certified renewable diesel for the relatively few extreme shifts that electric vehicles cannot cover. Copenhagen Airport has already adopted that approach, progressively electrifying its equipment while using HVO in compatible heavy vehicles, including snow-removal machines.

HVO is not unlimited, and its climate benefits depend on feedstock origin and production. Burning it also produces exhaust emissions. These constraints are important, particularly in populated areas. But a relatively small quantity used for exceptional winter duty is a different proposition from trying to replace a large share of road transportation with biofuels.

The hydrogen proposal must beat all these alternatives. It needs to demonstrate that the additional hours gained from the fuel cell are worth the vehicle cost, maintenance, fuel premium and refueling infrastructure. It also needs to outperform the cost of providing those hours with conventional generating equipment or retaining a small reserve fleet.

Snow-removal authorities have an obligation to maintain roads during severe weather. They should purchase equipment that meets that obligation with the lowest defensible whole-system cost and emissions. Norway has shown that batteries can perform demanding winter work, and China’s industrial scale is making specialized electric vehicles more accessible. Sweden’s hydrogen truck is entering a market in which the simpler electric solution is already working.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing analysis examines the operating results, procurement evidence, charging limitations, airport fuel-cell trials and the practical alternatives that make hydrogen’s business case so difficult.

#5740. Ford Teases Reborn Cobra R That Picks Up Where The Shelby GT350 Left Off

Folks, the Cobra is back. In a 36-second teaser posted by Ford Racing on X, the everything app, the Blue Oval said an "all-motor heart born from racing" is on the way for the Mustang, and if you read between the lines, "all-motor" means naturally aspirated. The engine audio clip playing in the background certainly lends credibility to that idea. With a 2027 launch date, there aren't any technical details to speak of, but the name "Cobra" gives me a lot of confidence this bad boy is going to sit above the GT and possibly even the Dark Horse.

You'll want to hear this. For the drivers, with an all-motor heart born from racing.  Ford Mustang Cobra, a Legacy Reborn.  The story continues in 2027. pic.twitter.com/fogI982jfl

— Ford Racing (@FordRacing) November 10, 2026

Of course, nothing is official, but leaked dealer information lends some credence to how this new Cobra will be positioned within the Mustang lineup. You can think of it as the "spiritual successor to the Mustang Shelby GT350," according to Ford Authority, and it'll launch next year as a 2028. Get it while you can, though, because it's expected to have a relatively short production run through the 2029 model year. Under the hood will be a naturally aspirated V8, obviously, and it's either going to be 5.2 or 5.4 liters, depending on how much freedom Ford feels like dispersing. Don't worry, it's also expected to have a Tremec six-speed manual transmission.

There's no word on horsepower numbers just yet, but we can look at the data as a guiding light. Currently, the Dark Horse's 5.0-liter V8 pumps out 500 horsepower and 418 pound-feet of torque. The Dark Horse SC takes those numbers all the way up to 795 and 660, respectively. Looking back, the 5.2-liter Voodoo V8 in the GT350 produced 526 hp and 429 lb-ft. If I were a betting man, I'd put my money on the horsepower number being somewhere around the 550-575 mark.

It has been quite a while since the Cobra name appeared on a Mustang from Ford. The last time it popped up was in the early 2000s supercharged SN95 Mustang SVT Cobra, which was a beast for the time. Since then, there have been some Shelby-specific Cobras, but nothing from Ford itself.

You may be asking yourself, "Why did Ford revive the name Cobra rather than just call the Shelby GT350's successor a Shelby GT350?" Well, it's because of money. As we explained earlier this year, Ford has to pay to use the name Shelby on its cars, and it doesn't want to anymore. Shelby America owns the name. It's the same reason the Dark Horse SC has its name rather than Shelby GT500. It hasn't been cheap, either. Ford was paying about $800 in royalties per Shelby Mustang it sold, racking up over $30 million in licensing fees in the process.

At the end of the day, it doesn't really matter what this thing is going to be called. Of course, "Cobra" is sick as hell, but it could be called the Ford Mustang Beige Wallpaper for all I care. It's going to be sick as hell.

#5739. Don't Overlook Cancer Risks in People With HIV, Experts Say

— Common cancers should be a key component of HIV care

Preventing and screening for common cancers seen in the general population should be a key component of HIV care, experts said at the recent IDWeek annual meeting.

Given cancer risks, "prevention becomes a key part of HIV care," noted Ma Somsouk, MD, of the University of California San Francisco, during a presentation at the meeting. That includes smoking cessation, treating hepatitis B and hepatitis C infection, managing diabetes and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, and screening for cancer.

Of note, AIDS-related cancers, including Kaposi sarcoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, are on the decline with improved therapies, but remain more common among people with HIV compared with the general population.

According to a Swedish retrospective case-control study, people with HIV were significantly more likely to develop human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated anal, penile, vulvar, and cervical cancers. An observational study showed that rates of oropharyngeal cancer among people with HIV have increased since 2000, particularly among heterosexual men ages 50 and older.

Somsouk noted that "the cancer burden is shifting with age in the HIV population." An estimated 70% of all people with HIV are 45 and older, he said, with greater risks of non-AIDS-related cancers like lung and prostate cancer.

Research has shown that people living with HIV have an increased risk for lung cancer, with some studies estimating risk to be 1.5 to 3-fold higher compared with the general population.

Furthermore, in a study of Medicaid beneficiaries, HIV was associated with a higher incidence of lung cancer (HR 1.75, 95% CI 1.56-1.96), with Black women at particular risk (HR 2.48, 95% CI 2.09-2.95).

While declining lung cancer deaths in the U.S. are tied to lower smoking prevalence, smoking risk among people with HIV remains "astronomical," said Chyke Doubeni, MD, MPH, of the Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center in Columbus, at the IDWeek annual meeting.

A 2016 meta-analysis showed that while 20% of U.S. adults smoked, more than half of people with HIV (54%) smoked -- and that rate rose to 74% among those with HIV and injection drug use.

Lung cancer screening among those with HIV isn't a one-time visit, Doubeni noted. Instead, it's a process that includes prevention, detection, and follow-up care. For clinicians, documenting the smoking history of a patient with HIV is the crucial first step in the prevention process, he said, followed by directing patients to smoking cessation resources.

Understanding how screening recommendations may differ, and how to apply their criteria to patients is also important.

For anyone ages 50 to 80 years with a 20 pack-year smoking history who smokes or quit in the last 15 years, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends annual lung cancer screening with low-dose CT. But Doubeni cautioned that many patients who die from lung cancer don't meet those criteria.

Recent American Cancer Society guidelines dropped the 15-year look-back and widened the potential screenable population. Why? "If you quit 20 years ago, your risk is lower, but it doesn't actually go away," Doubeni explained.

People with HIV are at average risk for colorectal cancer and standard screening recommendations apply. In Somsouk's presentation at IDWeek, he recommended colorectal cancer screening at ages 45 to 75 for those with HIV, with any test recommended by the USPSTF.

"In general, the best test is the one that you can get your patient to complete," Somsouk noted. But patients who have a positive fecal immunochemical test need a colonoscopy within 6 months, he added.

As for other gastrointestinal cancers, Somsouk advised screening for esophageal cancer with upper endoscopy or a capsule test for HIV patients with chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease plus three or more risk factors. He also recommended Helicobacter pylori testing for those with dyspepsia, peptic ulcers, or a family history of gastric cancer, as well as in high-risk groups, including immigrants from high-incidence regions. For those with cirrhosis of any cause or chronic hepatitis B virus infection, he advised alpha-fetoprotein testing and ultrasound to screen for liver cancer.

#5738. Introducing the Waymo Accessibility Network UK: Co-Designing the Future of Autonomous Mobility

Today, we’re launching the Waymo Accessibility Network UK to inform the future of autonomous mobility in the UK and enable a more independent future of transport. Whether it’s travelling to work, visiting friends, attending an appointment or simply enjoying everything a place has to offer, everyone deserves the freedom to travel with confidence and independence. Getting around should be about possibility, not barriers, and fully autonomous driving technology can provide more people with independent means of travel.

“Establishing the Waymo Accessibility Network UK is a vital step in ensuring our rollout of autonomous technology in London is inclusive, equitable, and aligned with local needs,” says Chris Ludwick, Waymo Product Management Director. “Working hand-in-hand with our UK partners allows us to refine, test, and deploy solutions that give passengers the freedom of truly independent travel.”

Waymo’s Accessibility Network provides a forum for leading British disability advocates and charities to engage with our team in a consistent, two-way dialogue, ensuring that diverse voices within the UK’s disability community actively shape how our technology is deployed on UK streets. Waymo’s Accessibility Network UK is an extension of our longstanding commitment to inclusive mobility and how we continuously improve our service based on feedback from the disability community. That feedback lives within our product today, helping inform features like audio cues and vehicle-finding tools.

Robin Spinks, Head of Inclusive Design at the Royal National Institute of Blind People (RNIB) says: “RNIB warmly welcomes the Waymo Accessibility Network, and we look forward to contributing alongside the blind and partially sighted community.”

London is a global leader in transport. But as we have been hearing from UK accessibility groups over many years, getting around can still present daily challenges, in particular for disabled and older passengers. For sight impaired Londoners commuting at peak times, finding the right vehicle on a busy street can be difficult. Guide dog users still face refusals in private hire vehicles. For older passengers and people with different physical or cognitive needs, even seemingly small aspects of a journey can make a significant difference. As we shared in our Vision for London, opening travel to all matters – and autonomous driving technology offers the opportunity to rethink some of these experiences.

The Waymo Accessibility Network will work directly with member organisations to support user research and participate in product testing. The feedback from members helps inform the passenger experience of our fleet and build upon Waymo’s current accessible design features, including:

We are honoured to collaborate with an exceptional group of national and community-based organisations that champion inclusion across physical, sensory, and cognitive disabilities. We welcome our 10 inaugural participants: RNIB, Re-Engage, AgeUK, Transport for All, Thomas Pocklington Trust, Guide Dogs UK, Sense, Motability Foundation, National Centre for Accessible Transport and Scope.

“Autonomous technology offers enormous potential to transform independent travel, but it must be shaped by disabled people from day one. By joining the Waymo Accessibility Network UK, NCAT hopes to ensure that disability-centred design sits right at the heart of the UK’s autonomous vehicle future.” says Clive Gilbert, Consortium Board Member at the National Centre for Accessible Transport and Head of Accessible Transport at Policy Connect.

“Thomas Pocklington Trust is delighted to be joining the Accessibility Network, along with other disability stakeholders. It is important that the voices of blind and partially sighted people are heard and that travelling in a Waymo can become a reality as the autonomous vehicle improves its accessibility, safety and other features. We want to build confidence for blind and partially sighted people, with independent travel on all modes of transport,” says Bhavini Makwana, Policy and Campaigns Lead at the Thomas Pocklington Trust.

Technology alone doesn’t remove every barrier. True accessibility depends on the streets we share, the vehicles we ride in, and the passengers we support. While Waymo can offer a major leap forward in independent mobility, we’ll always have more to learn. Bringing Waymo to the UK means doing so in partnership. As we work towards welcoming our first passengers in London, our goal is that Waymo becomes a trusted and valuable addition to the UK’s existing and iconic transport networks, and provides a new mobility option. Through Waymo’s Accessibility Network UK, we are ensuring that the people who experience barriers to mobility have a meaningful voice in shaping its future. We look forward to welcoming more UK organisations to the network as we work together to build safer, more inclusive streets for everyone.

#5737. Australia's Cheapest New Car Is This $13,000 MG Hatchback, And It's Far From A Stripper

Chinese cars have been beating down on long established performance and luxury car brands for a while now, all while costing a fraction of the price. From jumping over potholes to setting top speed records to beating Land Cruisers in off-road tests and even having emergency water travel capabilities, there are some mighty impressive pieces of kit across the Chinese car industry. What I'm most interested in, though, are the ultra-cheap economy cars that sell for the price of something used, and that's exactly what the MG3 offers to Australian car buyers. It's a compact hatchback with the face of a plecostomus, which isn't especially exciting, but its $13,020 USD price sure is.

It's no stripper, either. That bargain price includes features like Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, steering wheel controls, air conditioning, a digital driver's display, an auto-hold function, automatic power window switches, and adaptive cruise control with lane centering. It even has a standard feature that the new Toyota RAV4 doesn't even offer on its most expensive trim level that happens to be four times the price of the MG3: padded front and rear armrests. OK, so the MG3's actual MSRP in Australia is $13,890.85 USD at current exchange rates, but the fact that a dealer was even willing to discount it further is remarkable, too.

As you can see from CarSauce's review, the MG3 is woefully slow. Its 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine sends just 109 horsepower and 105 pound-feet of torque to the front wheels via a continuously variable transmission, which results in a leisurely 0-to-62 mph time of 12.57 seconds. It ain't quick, but it gets the job done, and again, it's a $13,000 car. The last car sold in the United States that was near the $13,000 mark was the diminutive Chevrolet Spark, which ran the 0-to-60 sprint in 10.8 seconds in Car and Driver's testing, so the MG3 isn't too far off that pace. Plus, looking beyond straight-line speed (or lack thereof), the reviewer even says it rides great and handles respectably, which are not always the case with bargain-basement cars.

Sadly the MG3's weak engine doesn't equate to exceptional fuel efficiency, with the presenter's real-world economy equating to about 36 mpg on the highway and more like 26 mpg around town. Those aren't abysmal numbers, just perhaps not as good as one might hope from such a weak engine in a tiny car.

Beyond the lower-than-low base price, the MG3's value proposition really comes into focus when you take into account its 10-year manufacturer warranty. For those who say, "why spend $13,000 on the cheapest new car available when you can buy a bigger, better used car for the same price?" Consider the idea of spending $13,000 on a car with a 10-year-long warranty versus spending that same amount on a used car with no warranty. The new car comes with an entire decade of mechanical coverage so the buyer doesn't have to worry about unexpected repair costs for those 10 years, whereas the used car could end up requiring costly repairs within the first year of ownership.

There are some quality concerns noted in the video, including infotainment software glitches and some apparent inconsistencies in the operation of those fancy automatic windows, but considering the price and that stellar warranty, I'd say the pros outweigh the cons in this case. For those who view their cars as another appliance, or those who simply want the financial security of not worrying about repair costs for a whole decade, the MG3 must be a pretty tempting option. Provided you live in Australia, of course — or Mexico, Europe, the Middle East, or other parts of the world where it's pretty damn cheap, too.

#5735. Tesla 'Full Self-Driving' One Step Closer To Recreating Human Driving By Overtaking Bicycles, Exceeding Speed Limits And Misidentifying Road Signs

Humans are imperfect, so at least in theory, robotaxis are supposed to save us by doing all the perfect driving we aren't able to do. Of course, had we poured every dollar that's been spent on robotaxi development into improving public transportation, self-driving cars would feel unnecessary. But the bigger problem is, after all those billions of dollars and years of development, Momentum Mag reports that a recent test of Tesla's so-called "Full Self-Driving" software found that it loved to speed through neighborhoods, illegally pass cyclists, and break other traffic laws. So basically, it drives like your least-favorite neighbor.

Woke 3 already killed the Cybertruck, so Tesla's school bus-passing software could be next on the chopping block after liberals figure out how to make every man a little shorter every time he disappoints a woman. Until then, it's important to know how good or bad the software controlling some of the most popular new cars actually is, which is why Belgian mobility organization johanna.be put the software to the test and found it frequently breaks speed limit laws in areas where drivers are most likely to hit pedestrians or cyclists. So that's not great.

Additionally, while there aren't many places in the U.S. where drivers can't legally pass a cyclist, that isn't the case in Belgium. You'd think fine-tuning the software to account for changes in laws between countries would have been a pretty basic part of Tesla's development, but nope. In johanna.be's testing, it found that Tesla's FSD system "repeatedly tries to overtake cyclists in cycle streets, something that is explicitly illegal in Belgium."

Coincidentally, right around the time johanna.be published the results of its Tesla safety test, the European Transport Safety Council shared the results of a separate safety test. The ETSC found that Tesla's "speed offset" and "contextual max speed" features don't follow United Nations or European Union rules regarding safety, and it's called on member states to reject both features later this year when the EU plans to hold an important vote on advanced driver assistance system regulation.

The ECF is also asking the EU to create a European Road Safety Agency that would act as "an independent EU body able to investigate issues involving automated systems and share the subsequent findings with other Member States." Even before the ETSC got involved, johanna.be's findings were concerning enough to warrant some serious attention from international regulators that Elon Musk wasn't able to gut. As the ECF put it, Tesla's so-called "Full Self-Driving" software (emphasis is the ECF's):

If a human loved to drive at 150% of the posted speed limit, regularly told people the speed limit was higher than it was, and kept trying to make illegal passes, we'd take their license and tell them to take the bus. With robotaxis and cars with driver-assist systems, it should be the same. Until they can prove they actually follow the rules of the road, there's no reason to let them on our roads. We also shouldn't allow automakers to sell driver-assistance systems that haven't been proven safe, either. Even if you disagree, I don't think you need a PhD in traffic safety to understand the argument there.

That said, it's entirely possible that safety researchers are criticizing Tesla for mistakes that every automaker's software makes. The problem with that argument is that johanna.be ran the same test with a Citroën C3 that managed to correctly identify all seven speed limit signs. For comparison, the Tesla got six of the seven speed limits wrong. It only got one correct. Imagine not only being wrong, but being more wrong than the French. Self-immolation is probably the only option.

While we wait to see how the EU's member states vote, the ECF also noted that otherwise docile behavior is no excuse for Tesla's software behaving badly in other ways. As it noted:

the study also found that FSD behaved cautiously and courteously around pedestrians and cyclists in general, yielding early, giving space, and even slowing for a sleepy cat in the road! However, this should not compensate for a pattern of speeding and illegal overtaking in streets that are primarily designed for safe walking and cycling

#5734. Polestar Formula 2030 Concept Makes Us Hope Polestar Will Be Back In America By 2030

Chinese-owned Polestar was banned from selling cars in the U.S. back in June, and like a scorned ex showing you what you're missing after a breakup, it's now revealed one of the coolest designs in recent memory: the Formula 2030 concept car. Look at what they took from us.

It's got a low, wide, shooting brake shape. The big front door, little rear door setup is pure enthusiast bait, and the switchgear inside looks like it came straight off of professional audio equipment. The Formula 2030 isn't just a for-show concept car, either, because Polestar says it will indeed "point towards future design direction for the brand."

Specifically, "various design attributes" seen here will actually show up in the next-gen Polestar 2 and upcoming Polestar 7 compact SUV. The Formula 2030 is billed as a compact four-door sports car, not really fitting neatly into any existing segment. It sits lower than the Polestar 5 grand tourer, fits between the 2 compact sedan and 7 size-wise, and is probably closest to the Polestar 4 in spirit.

It already looks great at a glance, but things get way more interesting once you start opening stuff up. Both the hood and rear hatch open up clamshell-style, exposing the natural fiber composite chassis underneath and orange Öhlins dampers. The half-size rear doors are coach doors, giving the Formula no B-pillar and a huge opening when all doors are open.

Inside, a very curved instrument screen measuring 20 inches sits on top of the steering column while a 12.2-inch center touchscreen sits in the middle. That touchscreen can physically lower when the driver switches drive modes to Performance, and raise when the car is in Autonomous. Below this screen is an array of up to eight customizable rocker switches and knobs. You can swap the specific switches or knobs out, like you can with, say, a pro-grade video game controller, and their individual functions can also be configured to your liking. All four bucket seats sit low in the cabin and get inflatable bolsters and cushions for better support.

I've never really thought about how rare four-spoke wheels are, but looking at the 22s on this Polestar concept, I'm simultaneously sad that they aren't more common but also completely understand why that's the case. They're definitely weird, but I also sort of dig it?

It all adds up to a funky yet beautiful design that makes us hope Polestar will return to the U.S. market by the Formula 2030's namesake. Given the political conditions that led to its banning and how those tides are turning in this country, that scenario actually feels like a real possibility.

#5732. Assessing and Managing HIV's Higher Heart Disease Risks

— People with HIV are twice as likely to develop cardiovascular disease

Understanding how HIV can shape cardiovascular disease risk may help clinicians tailor care to patients' needs, which starts with statins for most adults with HIV.

"HIV holds its own as a risk factor for developing cardiovascular disease," Virginia Triant, MD, MPH, of Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, said in a presentation at the IDWeek annual meeting.

A 2018 meta-analysis showed that people living with HIV were twice as likely to develop cardiovascular disease as those without HIV, Triant observed. Those with HIV also faced greater risks of myocardial infarction and stroke she added, putting HIV nearly on par with the cardiovascular relative risks found in the INTERHEART study for hypertension, diabetes, and smoking.

Traditional factors play a part in the elevated cardiovascular risks linked to HIV. People with HIV have greater rates of hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia than their HIV-negative counterparts, Triant noted. Research also shows an 85% lifetime history of smoking among those with HIV.

That doesn't explain the whole story, Triant pointed out. Antiretroviral therapy brings its own set of cardiovascular risks.

Early protease inhibitors like darunavir were linked with cumulative myocardial infarction risks, and recent use of the nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor abacavir was tied to increased myocardial infarction risk. It's not clear whether integrase strand transfer inhibitors also boost cardiovascular risk, with conflicting results from the RESPOND and HIV-CAUSAL studies.

After accounting for traditional risk factors and antiretroviral therapy, there's still a missing piece to the cardiovascular risk puzzle, Triant said. That piece may be the inflammation that comes with HIV.

The SMART study pointed to inflammation's role in cardiovascular disease, she noted. An analysis of data from the REPRIEVE study reinforced inflammation's role, even in people with well-controlled HIV and low to moderate cardiovascular risk.

Despite growing understanding of how HIV uniquely shapes cardiovascular risk, "this has not until very recently translated into differing and tailored clinical guidance for people with HIV," Triant stated. "I really see this as a challenge in delivering equitable care for cardiovascular care for people living with HIV."

Existing cardiovascular risk prediction scores for the general population fall short among people with HIV, incorporating only traditional risk factors without including HIV-related factors, Triant said. Even among those with HIV, cardiovascular risk varies by sex, race, ethnicity, and geographic location.

Among those with HIV, the Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) that debuted in 2013 underestimated cardiovascular risk in women and those in low to moderate risk groups. The more comprehensive 2023 PREVENT equations mirrored the PCE risk underestimation for people with HIV, with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) rates greater than PREVENT predictions.

Given underestimated risk, people with HIV have been less likely to receive cardiovascular preventive care that matches guidelines, Triant said. The guidelines for the general population are also less than what's needed for people with HIV, she said.

That began to change with cholesterol guidelines from the American Health Association (AHA) and other groups that added consideration of HIV as a cardiovascular disease risk factor. A 2019 AHA scientific statement that specifically focused on people with HIV highlighted risk-enhancing factors such as prolonged viremia, low CD4 counts, delays in starting antiretroviral therapy (ART), and metabolic syndrome.

Still, "what was really missing from the field was a large trial with robust data to support a recommendation for cardiovascular prevention for people with HIV," Triant said.

Then came REPRIEVE in 2023. That phase III clinical trial included only people with HIV on ART who had low to moderate cardiovascular disease risk and didn't meet general guidelines' thresholds for statin therapy. REPRIEVE showed that statin therapy was linked to a 36% reduction in MACE risk compared with placebo.

These results weren't driven by a subgroup. "It was reduction whether you looked by demographics, or traditional risk factors, or traditional HIV-related factors," Triant explained.

REPRIEVE was the first randomized trial that showed a cardiovascular prevention benefit that was different from the general population. "This is really paradigm-shifting," she noted. A CDC analysis found that full implementation of REPRIEVE's approach in people with HIV and low to moderate cardiovascular disease risk could lead to 7,418 fewer first major adverse cardiovascular events over 5 years.

The REPRIEVE findings have spurred practice-changing guidelines for people with HIV, Triant said.

In 2024, an HHS panel rolled out recommendations calling for daily moderate-intensity statins in people with HIV ages 40 to 75 years with low to intermediate (less than 20%) 10-year risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). In those with less than 5% risk, the HHS panel favored starting at least moderate-intensity statins.

The American College of Cardiology and other societies followed that with a dyslipidemia guideline in 2026 that recommended that everyone with HIV ages 40 to 75 years on ART receive statin therapy to reduce ASCVD event risk and slow coronary atherosclerosis.

"This is really a striking recommendation, and an important one for the field," Triant explained. "Notably, this is regardless of calculated baseline risk, regardless of LDL, for people in this age group."

Clinicians might want to consider starting statins at age 30 for those with HIV, she added. "I would strongly consider HIV to be an ASCVD risk enhancer, even at that age, even though we don't have the trial data," Triant said.

Even with these newly tailored guidelines, implementation will be a challenge, she noted. Statin uptake in people with HIV was suboptimal before REPRIEVE, with 80% of patients eligible for statins under earlier guidelines not getting them.

"Dismantling disparities that we know exist in cardiovascular prevention and care remains a critical challenge," Triant said. "The recent guidelines are likely to be practice-changing for people with HIV, but only if implemented on a broad scale."

#5730. Trump Administration Continues Systematic Dismantling of Public Lands

Proposed Rule Would Shut the Public Out and Allow the Administration to Make Sweeping Decisions About 250 Million Acres of Western Public Lands Behind Closed Doors

Yesterday, the Administration announced a proposed Bureau of Land Management (BLM) rulemaking that would drastically weaken the public’s involvement in land use planning and gut protections for Areas of Critical Environmental Concern (ACECs), one of BLM’s primary conservation designations, across 245 million acres of Western public lands. The rule proposes to stifle the voices of local communities by significantly shortening public comment periods and cutting out robust environmental analysis. These changes would make it easier for the BLM to fast-track the sale, transfer, or use of public lands for oil and gas drilling, mining, data centers, and other industrial or commercial development, all while shutting out the American people. The announcement kicks off a 60 day comment period (January 9th deadline).

The public lands overseen by the BLM contain crucial wildlife corridors, critical habitat, cultural resources and landscapes, watersheds, historic sites, and access to nature and scenery.  The rule threatens to strip vital safeguards for ACECs and environmental review that protect these values, leaving the West’s most sensitive lands vulnerable to irreparable harm.

This aggressive regulatory rollback is the latest chapter in a coordinated, systematic dismantling of America’s public lands. It directly connects to a broader pattern of hostility toward balanced stewardship, which includes the recent rescission of the landmark Public Lands Rule, stated intention to roll back the Roadless Rule and Wilderness policies, the evisceration of National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) standards, and repeated attempts to give away public lands to corporations and developers. This rulemaking contributes to this administration’s singular focus: fast-tracking industrial exploitation and drilling at the expense of our shared heritage, tribal sovereignty and the outdoor recreation economies that sustain rural Western communities.

The proposal comes as Congress debates permitting legislation that would also weaken public participation in decisions affecting shared lands and give more power to development interests.

Planning serves as the foundational blueprints governing public lands for decades; eroding these processes is a profound threat to the long-term health of the West. Making robust environmental review optional and weakening ACEC standards intentionally ties the agency’s hands, preventing it from effectively responding to the compounding threats of climate change, drought, and habitat fragmentation. This action rejects the unmistakable demand from the American public, including local leaders, Tribal representatives, and local elected officials, who have consistently called for public lands to be managed transparently and protected for future generations.

“The Trump Administration is once again plotting to undermine our world-renowned system of shared lands and the public processes that guide their management,” said Jackie Feinberg, Sierra Club’s National Lands Conservation Manager. “Weakening protections and public participation would fast-track the industrialization and privatization of places essential for wildlife, clean water, cultural and historic preservation, and access to nature. We stand firmly against these attempts to cut out the “public” from public lands for the benefit of corporate polluters and profiteers.”

“Gutting transparency, review, and public engagement requirements within the West’s most ecologically sensitive wildlife corridors, watersheds, and cultural resources are the actions of cowards trying to fast-track industrial development at any and all social costs,” said Kara Matsumoto, senior policy director at the Conservation Lands Foundation. “Resource management plans are the blueprints for keeping public lands and waters healthy, and weakening them will weaken local economies and fragile ecosystems. We’ll continue to fight this corporate greed because the overwhelming majority of Americans want more nature protected, not less.”

“The opportunity to review and comment on land management actions keeps the public in public lands.” said Hilary Eisen, federal policy director at Wild Montana. “Resource management plans provide the long-term framework for how vast swaths of public land across the West are managed and it is essential that these plans be crafted with robust public engagement. This proposed rule sidelines the public, as well as local, state, and tribal governments, in BLM land use planning.”

“Resource management planning is meant to provide the public a real say in how BLM manages our shared public lands, and Areas of Critical Environmental Concern are how the agency turns that input into on-the-ground protections for special places and important wildlife habitat,” said Maddy Munson, senior policy and planning specialist at Defenders of Wildlife. “Cutting back public participation and narrowing the agency’s analysis isn’t streamlining, but rather stacking the deck against the places and species that need protection the most.”

“For Nevadans public land is our way of life. Whether we have jobs dependent on mining, grazing, the outdoor industry or just love taking our families camping, these public lands in Nevada are a huge part of who we are. We want to have an active role in determining how these lands are managed and efforts to take the public out of this planning process and weaken protections are just wrong,” said Shaaron Netherton, Executive Director at Friends of Nevada WIlderness. “We need to stand up and keep the public in our public lands.”

“The Trump administration continues to eliminate tools that the Bureau of Land Management has relied on for decades for conserving wildlife habitat, protecting clean water, and working with local communities. The objective is clear: replace the multiple uses and values of our public lands with the singular use of fossil fuel development. That agenda has no footing in Colorado, where 96% percent of Coloradans support conserving public lands and open space and 81% believe oil and gas development is not an acceptable use of public lands,” said Juli Slivka, Senior Director of Policy and Programs at Wilderness Workshop.

“These are the plans that decide whether a valley gets drilled or a trout stream gets protected, and this proposal is built to make those decisions faster and with fewer people in the room,” said Bobby McEnaney, Senior Lands Analyst at NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council). “Cutting the public’s time to weigh in by two thirds, scrapping the full environmental review, and letting a political appointee invoke an emergency to skip the rest is not modernization. It is a way to lock in drilling and mining decisions before anyone can object. Governors get 30 days and no appeal, Tribal plans drop out of the review entirely, and the agency gives itself the power to shrink or erase existing protected areas. Interior should withdraw this proposal and keep the public’s seat at the table.”

“These lands are called “public lands” for a reason: They are owned by the people of the United States. The Bureau of Land Management’s job is to manage them in the public’s interest, for the common good. By so severely restricting opportunities for the public—including, importantly, Tribal Nations—to be involved in planning for their management, the BLM is depriving all of us of our rights as the owners,” said Michael Painter, Coordinator, Californians for Western Wilderness.

“The Trump administration continues its relentless agenda of handing over public lands to corporations,” said Thomas Delehanty, senior attorney with Earthjustice’s Rocky Mountain Office. “Cutting the public out of land management benefits no one except the extractive industries hellbent on controlling these shared resources for their own private gain. Anyone who values public lands must be loud and clear: these attacks end now.”

“Public lands belong to all Americans, and decisions about their future should be made through transparent processes informed by science, meaningful public participation and consultation with Tribes and others in the community. This proposed rule would give us less of a say in the management of 245 million acres of our shared lands and weaken areas of critical environmental concern, the BLM’s primary tool for protecting important natural and cultural sites. It is another clear attempt to give drilling, mining and other development interests more influence over our public lands, in the same spirit as rescission of the BLM Public Lands Rule—and only days after voters delivered a stinging rebuke to this administration’s agenda of doing favors for oil and gas companies and other powerful corporations. Our public lands deserve better, and so do future generations that will inherit them.” said Michael Carroll, BLM Campaign Director, The Wilderness Society.

“In New Mexico, the BLM planning process gives communities, Pueblos, Tribes, acequias, recreationalists, conservation organizations, ranchers, hunters and anglers a real say in what happens to the 13.5 million acres of public land that the agency manages here,” said Sally Paez, senior staff attorney for New Mexico Wild. “Places like the Greater Chaco landscape, the Permian Basin’s remaining wildlife habitat, and our desert grasslands have protections today because New Mexicans showed up and spoke out during planning. New Mexicans shouldn’t be shut out of decisions about their own public lands.”

“In Oregon, the BLM manages 2.6 million acres of Oregon and California Lands that are home to imperiled wildlife, endemic botanical resources, wild rivers, and climate change-mitigating ancient forests that provide outstanding recreational opportunities and socioeconomic benefits to Oregonians and all Americans,” said Susan Jane Brown, attorney with Silvix Resources. “The public and other stakeholders must have a central role in the science-informed stewardship of these cherished resources, all of which will be placed at risk of existential loss with BLM’s proposed rulemaking.”

“Oregon’s high desert community has modeled a long, successful history of federal planners, tribal interests, ranchers, hunters and anglers, recreationists, and conservationists working together to craft management strategies that balance land use and promote conservation across 12 million acres of our shared public lands,” said Mark Salvo, Senior Conservation Advisor for Oregon Natural Desert Association. “Now the Trump administration is recklessly dismissing these decades of collaboration and compromise, trampling public processes, and sidelining those who have worked to protect these lands and resources for future generations–all to advance a narrow agenda of exploitation at the expense of the public interest.”

“The public lands are the people’s lands and the American people have spoken loud and clear. The Bureau’s proposal to cut public participation, reduce protections for cultural sites and critically important habitat, and shortcut environmental analysis is just one more indication that the Trump Administration isn’t listening and will do anything to silence the public, Tribes, and scientists and ignore the reality of what’s happening on the ground,” said Josh Osher, public policy director for Western Watersheds Project. “Millions of acres of climate-stressed Bureau-managed lands are already being degraded by extractive industries, and we need planning rules that include thorough and honest science-based assessments and as many voices as possible to help improve ecological conditions and resilience.”

This is just the latest attempt from the Trump Administration to dismantle our public lands piece by piece,” said Sandra Schubert, Executive Director of Tuleyome. “The proposed Planning Rule undermines protections that ensure that our public lands and wild forests remain accessible and are used sustainably. Resource management plans are built on science and centuries of management experience. They give local land managers and communities the ability to maintain healthy ecosystems while supporting the diverse ways communities depend on public lands. Undermining planning undermines our public lands”

“Once again, Doug Burgum is doing everything in his power to cut the public out of public lands,” said Aaron Weiss, executive director of the Center for Western Priorities. “This new rule gives political appointees in DC more power to shrink protected places and ignore local voices. Public lands belong to all of us, and good land use planning means giving everyone the chance to weigh in.”

“America’s national parks are supported by the public lands that surround them, and this proposal is another blatant attempt to unravel decades of conservation progress that the public overwhelmingly supports,” said Beau Kiklis, associate director of energy and landscape conservation at the National Parks Conservation Association. “Roughly 80 national park sites share a border with BLM lands, and Areas of Critical Environmental Concern have helped protect Dinosaur National Monument from impacts of oil and gas development, support Joshua Tree’s wildlife by protecting the neighboring Pinto Mountains, and protect ancestral sites near Hovenweep among countless others. This is another attempt to sell off and sell out our public lands, and the public deserves a real say before more is lost.”

#5729. NASA Pushes Further Ahead With The Non-Space Side Of Its Mission, Teases New Experimental Plane

NASA has unveiled, sort of, its newest experimental plane. And by that, the agency appears to mean a plane meant to conduct experiments, rather than the plane itself being the experiment. Called the X-70 Fractal, the aircraft's primary selling point is its modular design, both inside and out. This means that payloads can be swapped out easily, whether they are hanging off the wings or nestled inside the plane. Even the flight controls can be reconfigured in case the agency wants to test different ways for the pilots (and it is piloted) to maneuver. The X-70 is really a platform to allow for a wide array of experiments on a single airframe, rather than creating a bespoke airframe to conduct one mission, like the X-59 is doing now.

As for the plane itself, the X-70 Fractal is... well, more announcement than vehicle, at least for now. NASA says that it can carry 2,000 pounds of science equipment and take off with up to 10,000 pounds total. It will fly up to 45,000 feet in altitude, far above most airliners and well into the stratosphere. It will go up to 1,500 nautical miles, broadly on par with an F-35. It also looks like an F-35, I think, maybe? For images, all we've got is this misty photo that looks AI generated. NASA seems to want to copy the energy of the F-47 and F/A-XX reveals, which are also foggy renderings and not actual photographs. Show me you're making an airplane without showing me you're making an airplane, I guess.

NASA achieves such historic feats in space that it's easy to forget that it is also an "Aeronautics" administration. Part of its remit is to push forward the boundaries of aviation here on this planet, which NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has renewed focus on. Isaacman himself is a pilot who owns his own MiG-29 Soviet fighter jet, so this is an area of personal interest for him. In fact, he's promising that more experimental aircraft are on their way; rumors abound that the agency may be returning the famous SR-71 Blackbird, the fastest plane ever made, to service.

By doing so, NASA does important R&D on airplane technology that is then released into the public record, to the benefit of all aviation companies and everyone who flies on their products. That's the whole point of the X-59, which is trying to reduce the impact of sonic booms enough to make commercial supersonic planes financially viable. In addition, NASA's latest budget points to aviation as an area of strategic competition, per Wired. To that end, it may do some research alongside the Pentagon as well. This is where something like the X-70 is useful: it could do scientific, commercial, or military research as needed, simply by swapping out equipment payloads via its modular design. Now all NASA needs to do is, you know, build it, possibly with a contractor. Details!

#5727. DOJ Slaps Lyft With $53 Million Lawsuit For Allegedly Discriminating Against Disabled Riders

The U.S. Department of Justice is suing ride-hailing company Lyft, accusing it of routinely discriminating against people with disabilities in direct violation of federal law. The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, alleges that Lyft and its drivers "routinely refuse to serve" people with disabilities, such as folks who use stowable wheelchairs or ride with service animals. The DOJ also accused the San Francisco–based company of imposing cancellation fees on people who were denied service and charging passengers with disabilities higher fees and unnecessary surcharges.

The Justice Department sought $53 million in damages for the "hundreds, and likely thousands" of customers it said Lyft and its drivers had wronged, and it's the latest in a series of legal actions the government has taken against major ride-hailing companies related to alleged Americans with Disabilities Act violations, according to Reuters. Just last year, the DOJ accused Uber of similar behavior and sought $125 million in damages. Uber says it has since committed to expanding access and improving the experience of riders with disabilities.

The department said Lyft failed to change its policies and practices to prevent this sort of discrimination, and it failed to adequately train drivers and customer service representatives about their obligations under federal law, The New York Times reports. On top of the $53 million in damages for passengers, the government is asking the court to consider a civil penalty against Lyft.

Uber, and now Lyft, have disagreed with the allegations vehemently. Here's what Lyft told The Times in a statement:

Discrimination has no place in the Lyft community. We have longstanding policies requiring drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or use foldable mobility devices, and drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation.

It should be noted that Lyft says it is fully cooperating with the Department of Justice through this entire process.

Unfortunately for everyone involved, this is not the first time Lyft has been in hot water over discriminating against folks with disabilities. As The Times points out, the company resolved allegations that its drivers denied services to people who used wheelchairs or walkers in 2020. Admittedly, the scope and penalties were far smaller back then, but it's a big deal nonetheless. Six years ago, it agreed to revise its policies and pay four passengers thousands of dollars in damages, along with a $40,000 civil penalty.

#5726. Novel Glucagon/GLP-1 Agonist Meets Cardiovascular Safety Endpoint

— Survodutide was noninferior to placebo for major adverse cardiovascular events, trial shows

Survodutide, an investigational glucagon receptor and GLP-1 receptor dual agonist, was safe for patients with obesity and either established cardiovascular disease (CVD), chronic kidney disease (CKD), or increased risk of CVD, a randomized trial found.

Among more than 5,500 patients, the primary composite endpoint -- death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal stroke, nonfatal myocardial infarction, ischemia-related coronary revascularization, or heart failure event -- occurred in 3.7% of those on survodutide versus 4.1% of those on placebo (P<0.0001 for noninferiority).

In the SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT trial, survodutide "met its primary endpoint, establishing cardiovascular safety by demonstrating noninferiority to placebo for MACE [major adverse cardiovascular events]," Biykem Bozkurt, MD, PhD, of Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, said during her presentation at the American Heart Association (AHA) annual meeting in Chicago.

This safety trial provides clinicians with "reassuring data" that treatment with the dual agonist is not associated with increased cardiovascular risk, Bozkurt and colleagues concluded in their report, published simultaneously in The Lancet.

"Given the novelty of this new incretin-based therapy class, establishing cardiovascular safety of glucagon receptor–GLP-1 receptor dual agonists through noninferiority trials is essential," the authors wrote, and has become an expectation by regulatory agencies both in the U.S. and Europe, Bozkurt added.

Treatment with survodutide was also associated with improvements in systolic blood pressure, waist circumference, HbA1C, body weight, lipid levels, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, Bozkurt said.

Gastrointestinal events and treatment discontinuations were more frequent during the dose escalation phase, she added. "Overall, the safety profile was consistent with that observed in the previously reported phase III trials with no unexpected safety findings," Bozkurt said.

AHA discussant Stephen Nicholls, MBBS, PhD, of Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, pointed out that the study design means that while cardiovascular harm can be excluded, "we cannot make any inference about cardiovascular benefit."

The findings raise the question of "what is important to stakeholders when we design our clinical trials?" Nicholls said. "From a regulatory perspective, it would seem it's a relatively low bar to simply show that there's no cardiovascular harm. We need to think more and more about how do we design clinical trials with what's important for our patients and the clinicians that they are working with."

The hope is to eventually triage the right patient to the right treatment at the right time in their disease process, Nicholls added, "and facilitate shared decision-making to achieve more effective personalized prevention of cardiovascular disease and obesity complications."

SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT was a global, phase III, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven, cardiovascular safety trial conducted at 524 sites in 34 countries. Adult patients were eligible if they had a body mass index of 27 kg/m2 or greater, and established CVD or at least two obesity complications or CVD risk factors. Participants with CKD were eligible if they had a BMI of 30 kg/m2 or greater.

A total of 5,530 patients were randomly assigned to a once-weekly dose of subcutaneous survodutide, up-titrated to 3.6 mg or 6.0 mg, or placebo. Of these, 5,507 were actually treated, equally divided between the three dosing arms.

Median time in the study was 22 months. At study close-out, 56.0% of the survodutide 3.6-mg group, 56.6% of the survodutide 6.0-mg group, and 59.0% of the placebo group were still on treatment.

Efficacy and safety analyses included all randomly assigned patients who received at least one dose of survodutide or placebo. The primary analysis, which pooled outcomes for both survodutide doses compared with placebo, was performed according to the treatment-regimen estimand, which assessed treatment effects "regardless of any early discontinuation of survodutide or placebo, temporary stop, the use of protocol-prohibited obesity medications, or a prolonged dose-escalation period," the authors noted.

A secondary three-point MACE endpoint -- death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal stroke, or nonfatal myocardial infarction -- occurred in 2.4% of 3,671 participants in the pooled survodutide group and 2.8% of 1,836 in the placebo group (P<0.0001 for non-inferiority).

Adverse events occurred in 93.0% of the 3.6-mg dose survodutide group, 93.1% of those in the 6.0-mg group, and 85.6% of those on placebo. Gastrointestinal events, including nausea and vomiting, were more frequent in the treated groups, and gastrointestinal events leading to discontinuation occurred in 19.3% of the 3.6-mg group, 20.8% of the 6.0-mg group, and 1.9% of the placebo group.

Serious adverse events and fatal adverse events were similar across treatment groups. Fatal events were primarily due to cardiac disorders, the authors noted.

#5724. At $17,000, Is This Meyers Manx SR2 A Super Cool Cat?

Today's Nice Price or No Dice Manx SR2 is the second VW-based kit car offered by legendary builder Bruce Meyers, and it features a design he thought would be far harder to copy than his first: the ubiquitous dune buggy. Let's decide what such a unique bit of car culture should cost.

With the recent discontinuation of the Supra, fans eager to carry the torch of non-tepid Toyotas are left with only the GR86 coupe and the crazily expensive GR Corolla as rides of choice. The fact that Toyota couldn't be bothered to develop the last-generation Supra on its own, leveraging BMW for most of the under-skirt bits, makes it questionable whether the company even has any interest in sporty cars anymore. Instead of pulse-pumping sports cars, the company offers around a dozen five-door crossover-style vehicles, since that's what sells these days.

That wasn't always the case; in addition to the Supra, Toyota once offered a rally-bred version of the stalwart Celica and a full-blown mid-engine sports car in the MR2. We looked at a 1993 Toyota MR2 on Tuesday, a non-turbo car that otherwise had all the options we'd want. Unfortunately, that non-turbo nature and a non-working A/C compressor called into question its $14,000 asking price. In the end, you all gave that a heave-ho in an 85% 'No Dice' downvote.

A lack of taint-tightening Toyotas doesn't mean that the automotive landscape has totally turned into dullsville, however. There are plenty of fun and interesting cars and, yes, even trucks, out there from which to choose when something more than sleepwalking self-driving is in order. But what if you wanted something crazier than what's on the menu right now from the ever-shrinking cadre of entertaining cars on the market? That's when a rare opportunity like today's Meyers Manx SR feels especially apt.

The SR2's creator, Bruce Meyers, grew up living the California dream. A bohemian artist and engineer, Meyers spent his early adult years surfing, off-road racing, and teaching himself to mold fiberglass as a boat builder. His talents all merged in the creation of the original Meyers Manx dune buggy, introduced in 1964.

Built on a VW Type 1 platform shortened by 14.5 inches, the Manx immediately became an icon and set off an industry of copycats. Meyers went to court to stop the copiers from making dime on his design, but to little success. Taking another tack, Meyers' next street kit, the Manx SR2 (Street Roadster), was far more complex, featuring 10 body panels (as opposed to the original Manx's two) and iconic scissor-style doors. Unfortunately, the cost of the lawsuits, along with nasty letters from the IRS, ate away at Meyers' company finances, and he closed the doors in 1971. By that time, fewer than 200 Manx SR body kits had left the Fountain Valley factory.

This is one of those rare SR models, built on a VW Beetle platform, but powered by a Chevy Corvair air-cooled six. Unlike most automotive engines, the Corvair mill spins counterclockwise, so the car also has the Chevy four-speed manual gearbox instead of a VW transmission. According to the ad, the added power (likely around 140 horsepower gross) makes the car "fly!"

The car rolls, appropriately enough, on a set of Western Bullet Torque Thrust-style wheels wrapped in white-letter BF Goodrich tires. They sit proud in the exaggerated wheel arches, looking almost comically large in comparison to the car's miniature 80-inch wheelbase.

Another way Bruce Meyers and co-designer Stewart Reed sought to improve upon the original Manx was through weather protection, fitting the SR2 with an optional fabric targa top and side curtains. This car appears to have neither, nor does it even seem to have a windshield wiper, making it a fair-weather friend. It's also missing one of the front bumperettes, which could be hard to find. Other than those issues, the car's exterior appears to be in really good shape, with the paint still shining and everything else still intact.

Make no mistake, though: this car is a project that needs some work. The seller claims the seats are "ready for upholstery," implying that they have somehow been pre-gaming for the effort. There's also apparently an issue with the scissor doors (a first, by the way), as they seem to be sitting in place in most of the pictures but aren't actually attached by their hinges. That's evident in the interior photo, where the passenger-side door is absent entirely.

The interior itself is in rough but serviceable condition. Those upholstery-ready seats are nothing more than fiberglass shells with an inch or so of ancient foam padding, and they look about as comfortable as sitting on an orange crate. The rest of the cabin is black-painted fiberglass with a bare VW floorpan. Neither element looks too egregious.

The dashboard offers a full complement of VDO gauges with the tach hilariously pegged at a 4,500 rpm redline. The speedometer's odometer inset shows 30,461 miles, but the ad claims an "I don't know" 99,999 as the mileage. On the plus side, the car's title is clean, and the seller claims it is licensed as an "asvr," which I believe means home-built, with a 1987 VIN assignment.

As noted at the outset, this Manx SR is one of those rare birds to catch in the classifieds. It's not crazy rare, though, as there's another with the same Corvair power, but in orange and with a salvage title, offered through one of the classic car classifieds.

This one, despite some questions and missing pieces, looks like a great foundation for a light restoration. That would result in a unique and fun sport-about for weekend and car show duty. Find the top and side curtains, and rain won't be the hindrance the car currently faces.

With all that in mind—and yes, it was a lot—what do you think about this Manx SR? More importantly, how do you feel about spending $17,000 to buy it? Is that a fair price, given the car's rarity and condition? Or does that price make you want to turn tail and run?

Los Angeles, California, Craigslist, or go here if the ad disappears.

#5722. What New Car Excites You The Most?

Despite the fact that new or redesigned cars are announced seemingly every day, it's not a given that they're especially exciting. Different people find different things exciting, too, so it's not an objective measure, but it's an important factor in why people choose to buy a car in the first place. Whether you're in the market for a new car or not, we want to know, what new car excites you the most? Sound off in the comments section below to share your answer with your fellow Jalops.

For the most part, Americans are facing financial difficulties at the moment, from the raging affordability crisis to absurdly high fuel prices and a litany of other challenges, so maybe your view of an exciting car is one that's actually affordable for the average Joe. Maybe you love small cars so you're stoked on the Scion by Toyota KEI-01, or you're a horsepower addict who is more excited about the C8 Corvette Grand Sport's new 6.7-liter V8. There are no wrong answers, we just want to know what new car excites you the most.

The new car that excites me the most is the new Rivian R2. It's no secret that the Tesla Model Y sells like hotcakes, but I find it encouraging to see that a different American automaker that's not run by the world's richest and most narcissistic man can also produce an appealing, affordable, and effective competitor. I love Rivian's design language, and I think the R2 is super cool and looks truly distinctive when compared to other compact SUVs.

A fully loaded R2 Performance AWD Launch Edition rings in at about $60,000. For that price you get a whopping 656 horsepower and 609 lb-ft of torque, which is good enough for 0-to-60 sprints of around 3.5 seconds while still providing around 330 miles of range. Plus, its rear window rolls down like a Toyota 4Runner, a fantastic feature that I think more cars should have.

I think it will provide a genuinely wonderful ownership experience for thousands of buyers, and maybe even spark the next generation of car enthusiasts, which is truly exciting. But that's enough from little old me, you're here for you and your fellow Jalopnik readers! Head down to the comments section and share which new car excites you the most.

#5721. Impeach and Remove RFK Jr.

— The incoming Congress has several avenues to pursue Secretary Kennedy's impeachment

When the new Congress convenes on January 3, 2027, Secretary of HHS Robert F. Kennedy Jr. should be impeached by the House of Representatives and then removed by the Senate.

Can this be done? Yes. Although classically associated with presidents, impeachment applies equivalently to federal officials. The House votes to impeach by a simple majority, which triggers a Senate impeachment trial. Removal occurs if two-thirds of senators agree the official engaged in "...treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors."

Just two cabinet secretaries have been previously impeached, the most recent being Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024. Also of note, articles of impeachment already were filed against Kennedy in 2025 by Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.).

Impeachment can serve many purposes even without removal: the personal and professional embarrassment of the impeached official or to bring information to light through document discovery and the compelled testimony. Politicians can also grandstand during impeachments and drive points home for votes. For example, when the House impeached Secretary Mayorkas in 2024, his probability of removal was zero as the Senate was controlled by the other party, which opposed his impeachment. A trial of merits then never even occurred as the Senate voted to dismiss. As a result, the process was arguably performative.

The goal of Kennedy's impeachment would be removal from office because he is dangerous to public health -- because without it, more Americans will needlessly suffer and die. That is the only goal in my mind.

Which Arguments Could Kennedy's Impeachment be Based Upon?

Several options exist to pursue Kennedy's impeachment. All appear valid, and we don't have to select just one, though each also has strengths and weakness, pros and cons.

One avenue is looking at dereliction of duty, particularly in our ongoing measles outbreak. The number of American measles deaths should be zero. It was zero for years, and safe, effective vaccination exists. A single measles death is an unacceptable tragedy laid at the feet of pernicious leaders such as Kennedy. Now, the U.S. is on the brink of losing its measles elimination status, pending the outcome of the Pan American Health Organization meeting.

These arguments mirror those of Mayorkas' impeachment alleging incompetence at managing the southern border, therefore endangering Americans. It's also emotionally resonant as we are all watching the measles outbreak stack caskets in real time.

But "dereliction" and "competence" could prove qualitative rather than explicitly provable. Kennedy, for example, could claim that HHS is doing its best though measles is simply an intractable foe.

A stronger argument may thus lie in his cancellation of $8.9 billion in biomedical research grants. Unlike degrees of dereliction, grant cancellation is an unassailable fact that violates Congress' "power of the purse" as the funds had been earmarked. Regardless of party, if Congress approves funds for an expenditure then the expenditure should be discharged. For congressionally funded programs, the executive branch is executor, not executioner.

The administration's multi-front assault on research draws less attention than deserved given its long-term harm. A generation of medical scientists is being kneecapped, laboratories are shuttering, universities reeling. This magnitude of harm is incalculable because it is unknown -- what are the future cures that are now lost?

Even if impeachment proceeds, Kennedy's removal is a separate question. Removal in the Senate requires 67 votes; an admittedly high bar, never before achieved. The new Senate makeup is still pending narrow races. However, the final party distribution also shouldn't matter, as removal cannot be partisan in the first place. At 67 votes, removal will require both parties, so a politically centered impeachment would end with Kennedy still secretary. But questions of basic competence and our country's health should not be partisan.

Would a sufficient number of senators from both parties vote to remove? One lesson hopefully learned in this midterm election is that, regardless of party, politicians embrace unpopular figures at their peril, and Kennedy is deeply unpopular. The anti-vaccination movement is disproportionately loud, especially with conspiracists now in positions of power, though this fundamentally misrepresents voters' overwhelming support of vaccines. So, an electoral argument could resonate with a senator on either side of the aisle.

Kennedy's anemic support would likely further erode through the discovery process if impeachment proceeds. He's performed dismally during prior congressional testimony, as one would expect from someone with no formal training -- or even real-world work experience -- in healthcare, medicine, or science. The new Congress is on track for a record number of physicians, with doctors who support vaccination sitting on both sides of the aisle in both chambers. How many times have physicians, called before Congress, faced grilling from legislators who are lawyers? Now a lawyer, Kennedy, may face questions from leaders who are doctors.

So, is removal ultimately likely? To be frank, no, it remains definitively uphill. But it's worth pursuing.

Several counterarguments to impeachment exist, including the discretion given to the executive branch in managing agencies and the fact that senators previously voted for instatement while well aware of Kennedy's conspiratorial incompetence. There's also genuine concern for establishing precedent in which future secretaries become routinely impeached by opposing parties. Prior to 2024 there had only been one executive impeachment, and now there could be two in short order. (Meanwhile, the recent effort to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was blocked.) And finally, the effort would be an uphill battle, with the risk of Kennedy emerging stronger should removal fail.

But Kennedy is a historically dangerous individual. How many deaths emanate from his secretaryship and how many more will die if his power is left unchecked? In our work every day, doctors bravely contemplate actions for which we balance risk against the possibility of lives saved if successful. This is no different. Impeachment is fraught, and there are risks, but we have, in the coming months, a window of opportunity with action demanded by the net calculus of consequences.
