#5659. Opinion: Low-income parents can’t afford to take chances with nutritious food their picky eaters might reject

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

By Priya Fielding-Singh and Darcy Cherlin

Fielding-Singh is the director of policy and programs at the Global Food Institute at the George Washington University. Cherlin is the research project manager at the Global Food Institute at the George Washington University.

As high food costs and cuts to food assistance squeeze families’ budgets, concerns are growing about whether low-income parents will be able to keep putting food on the table.

But these financial pressures threaten to do more than increase hunger. They also risk harming children’s diets and health in the long run — by making nutritious foods not only harder to afford, but also increasingly risky for parents to buy.

To understand why, consider the most universal of parenting frustrations: picky eating. Most parents experience it, but the stakes vary widely. For well-off parents, watching a child push away a helping of vegetables is annoying but manageable. A carrot left untouched one day can simply mean trying again the next.

But for parents living close to the bone, that same rejected carrot is more than frustrating. It represents money that could have been spent on something their child would have actually eaten.

Simply put: Children’s food refusals come at a cost — one that few cash-strapped families can afford.

Such financial risks profoundly shape how low-income parents feed their kids, as sociologists have documented for years. A decade ago, Caitlin Daniel first showed how the risk of wasting money on rejected nutritious foods led low-income parents to prioritize buying less healthy items they knew their kids would eat. Years later, one of us (Priya) found that catering to kids’ preferences was also driven in part by parents’ earlier bouts of food insecurity: Determined to spare their children those experiences, caregivers often relied on familiar, comforting foods they knew would fill their kids’ stomachs.

Our newest study adds another dimension to this picture. Low-income parents across three states described going to considerable lengths to prioritize children’s nutrition, often at the expense of their own diets.

At the same time, to conserve resources and keep dinnertime from turning into a battle, they paid close attention to their kids’ likes and prioritized buying what they knew their children would eat. As one mother put it, she’d rather her daughter be “happy and fed than sad and hungry.”

Within such severe financial constraints, catering to children’s preferences is strategic. But it can also undermine children’s diets and health over time. That’s because raising kids to be healthy eaters is a long game: Children’s tastes develop gradually as they encounter and become familiar with different foods, and young children often need to try unfamiliar, healthier ones — like bitter vegetables — multiple times before accepting them.

That’s why pediatricians and nutrition experts routinely encourage parents to keep offering fruits and vegetables, even when kids turn them down. It’s smart advice, but it assumes parents can shoulder the costs of following it.

For families with little money to spare, doing so has always been a gamble. And today, it’s becoming an even bigger one. Groceries now cost nearly a third more in dollar terms than they did in 2020. Meanwhile, participation in SNAP — the nation’s largest food assistance program — has fallen by over 5 million people, including an estimated 2 million children, since summer 2025.

These economic pressures are now showing up in parents’ food decisions. A national survey found that more than half of low-income parents reported cutting back on groceries, while over two-thirds worried about having to choose between paying bills and buying healthy food for their children.

Forcing parents into such trade-offs doesn’t just threaten their ability to keep children fed. It also undermines their efforts to help children eat — and learn to enjoy — nutritious foods.

Fortunately, there are ways to address both problems.

First and foremost, we need to ensure children have enough to eat. That means restoring access to food assistance. The next Congress should reverse the cuts to SNAP enacted through H.R. 1 and stop SNAP benefit costs from being shifted to states — a shift that could jeopardize continued access to a program millions of families depend on to put food on the table. To make a bill reversing the cuts veto-proof, it should be a bipartisan effort.

But we also need to invest in programs that support parents’ efforts to feed their children nutritious foods, including incentives that make those purchases more affordable and less financially risky. Protecting and strengthening WIC’s fruit and vegetable benefit and expanding produce incentives like Double Up Food Bucks for SNAP recipients can help families stretch their grocery dollars further, giving them more room to buy nutritious foods their children might not eat the first time around.

Schools and childcare programs must also be critical partners in this work. Beyond providing nutritious meals, they can give kids regular opportunities to encounter and try healthier foods without leaving parents to shoulder the full financial burden. Expanding initiatives like the Department of Agriculture’s Fresh Fruit and Vegetable Program and Farm to School programs, which help introduce children to new foods through fresh produce, taste tests, gardens, and other activities, can help.

Nutrition experts are right to encourage parents to keep introducing healthy foods, even when their children refuse them. But advice that families can’t afford to follow simply won’t cut it. We need food policies that not only ensure children have enough to eat, but also give parents the resources and support to help them develop healthy eating habits that last.

Priya Fielding-Singh is the director of policy and programs at the Global Food Institute at the George Washington University and the author of “How the Other Half Eats: The Untold Story of Food and Inequality in America.” Darcy Cherlin is the research project manager at the Global Food Institute at the George Washington University.

#5658. Oura to acquire AI virtual primary care partner Counsel Health for $625M

Oura to acquire AI virtual primary care partner Counsel Health for $625M" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Smart ring maker and health tracking company Oura plans to acquire AI virtual primary care company and business partner Counsel Health for $625 million, the health tech companies announced Tuesday.

The all-cash deal is expected to close before the end of this year, pending customary closing conditions. Bringing Counsel’s platform and capabilities in-house will allow more Oura members to bring their biometric data into a virtual, in-app care encounter, the companies said in their announcement.

“Oura helps members understand their physiology and, with Counsel, they can take action on their health across a range of needs, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care and referrals,” Tom Hale, CEO of Oura, said. “Together, we can create a new model of care that extends the current healthcare paradigm by delivering an experience that’s more immediate, personalized, and proactive. This is a massive step in our mission to empower people to live healthier, longer, by delivering on the promise of a 24-7 doctor in your pocket.”

Counsel’s model uses text-based, records-informed medical AI encounters to help field and triage users, providing a path to telehealth encounters with the company’s in-house physicians, who are also supported on the backend by a proprietary “Clinician Cockpit” that surfaces relevant clinical data for the encounter. The two-year-old company boasts enterprise partnerships with health plans, provider organizations, employers and other consumer health organizations, for whom it says its approach can reduce costs and improve access to timely care.

Oura is a digital health giant with 5.7 million paid members, whose recently postponed IPO was targeting a $15.6 billion valuation. The company says it is profitable and “growing meaningfully” with 92% year-over-year revenue growth (nearly $1.8 billion) for the fiscal year ended Sept. 30, but ultimately delayed the offering due to “uncertainty” in the market. Its most recent fiscal quarter, ended Sept. 30, included 153% year-over-year revenue growth and an adjusted EBITDA of $87 million.

Oura has partnered with Counsel since June, and in September, announced a tighter collaboration centered on the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ ACCESS (Advancing Chronic Care with Effective Scalable Solutions) Model, set to begin early next year. The companies have said early data from their partnership show strong care satisfaction among those who saw a physician (4.6 out of 5 average rating), widespread agreement among Counsel members (90%) that use of their Oura data helped improve care, and general Oura member satisfaction (70%) with the onboarding to Counsel’s services.

“At Counsel, we’ve built medical AI around trust, safety and responsibility, keeping physicians in the loop for clinical decisions,” Muthu Alagappan, M.D., founder and CEO of Counsel, said in the announcement. “Oura’s data gives clinicians objective context, trended biometrics, and member engagement to deliver more informed care. From the start, our teams bonded over a joint vision, shared culture and mission, further solidifying as we negotiated our deal over the past few months.”

Under a new owner, the company will continue to serve its existing enterprise partners while expanding to new customers and broadening its clinical capacity. For the latter, Oura and Counsel said they plan to bolster preventive care via continuous monitoring and proactive guidance; acute care via timely intervention for episodic health issues; and specialty and chronic care management in areas like reproductive health, cardiometabolic health and aging.

“Oura tells members what’s happening in their bodies, and Counsel helps them act on it,” summarized Oura Executive Chairperson David Shuman. “This combination expands our addressable market and deepens the value we deliver to every member. This not only increases lifetime value, but Counsel’s enterprise partners also open the door to millions of people beyond our existing member base.”

#5657. Scientists discover surprising heart benefits of eating avocado and mango every day

Eating mango and avocado every day could offer unexpected benefits for heart health, according to new research. In a study lasting just eight weeks, adults with prediabetes who regularly ate both fruits experienced improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure, without gaining weight or consuming more calories.

The findings could be especially relevant to the one in three (98 million) Americans with prediabetes, a condition in which blood sugar levels are elevated but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, the research suggests that incorporating these two nutrient-rich fruits into everyday meals may help support cardiovascular health.

Researchers at Illinois Institute of Technology (Illinois Tech) investigated the effects of an Avocado-Mango (AM) diet that included one medium Hass avocado and one cup of fresh mango each day. Participants followed this eating plan for eight weeks, while a comparison group consumed a similar diet in which the fruits were replaced with carbohydrate-based foods containing equivalent calories.

The results revealed notable differences between the groups, particularly in how well their blood vessels functioned and how their blood pressure changed over time.

One of the clearest improvements involved the ability of blood vessels to expand as blood flows through them. This flexibility helps maintain healthy circulation and is an important indicator of cardiovascular health.

To evaluate this response, researchers measured flow-mediated dilation (FMD), a commonly used test of endothelial function (blood vessel health). The endothelium is the thin layer of cells lining the inside of blood vessels, where it helps regulate circulation and the widening and narrowing of arteries.

Among participants eating avocado and mango, the measurement increased significantly to 6.7%. In contrast, it declined to 4.6% in the control group. The difference suggests that regularly consuming these fruits may help blood vessels function more effectively.

Blood pressure measurements also showed encouraging changes, especially among male participants. Men in the control group experienced an average increase of 5 points (mmHg) in central blood pressure, while those consuming avocado and mango saw a reduction of approximately 1.9 points.

Diastolic blood pressure, the lower number in a blood pressure reading, reflects the pressure inside arteries when the heart relaxes between beats. Maintaining healthy levels is important because elevated blood pressure can place additional strain on the cardiovascular system. Researchers noted that the differences observed in the study could be clinically meaningful if they persist over time.

Importantly, the cardiovascular improvements occurred without significant changes in participants' body weight or total calorie consumption. This suggests that the nutritional quality of the foods people eat may influence heart health even when their weight remains stable.

“This research reinforces the power of food-first strategies to help reduce cardiovascular disease risk, particularly in vulnerable populations like those with prediabetes,” said Britt Burton-Freeman, PhD, Principal Investigator and Professor at Illinois Tech. “It’s an encouraging message: small, nutrient-dense additions—like incorporating avocado and mango into meals and snacks—may support heart health without the need for strict rules or major dietary overhauls.”

Beyond the improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure, participants eating mango and avocado consumed more fiber, vitamin C, and monounsaturated fat. These nutrients are associated with cardiovascular wellness and may help explain some of the observed benefits.

Researchers also identified improvements in certain indicators of kidney health, including estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), a measurement used to assess how effectively the kidneys filter waste from the blood.

However, the fruits did not produce significant improvements in every health measurement. Cholesterol levels, blood sugar, and markers of inflammation remained largely unchanged compared with the control group.

Together, the results suggest that regularly including nutrient-rich fruits in the diet could be a practical way to support cardiovascular health, particularly for people with prediabetes who face an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

Although mango and avocado have very different flavors and nutritional profiles, they provide complementary nutrients that support several aspects of cardiovascular and metabolic health.

Mango provides dietary fiber (2g/serving, 7% DV, Mango serving size: ¾ cup) and is an excellent source of vitamin C (50% DV). Vitamin C is an antioxidant that helps protect cells from damage, while fiber contributes to healthy digestion and may help with blood sugar regulation, weight management, and cardiovascular wellness.

Avocado offers another combination of potentially beneficial nutrients. It contains fiber (3g/serving, 11% DV, Avocado serving size: 50 g (1/3 of a medium avocado)), which plays a role in managing cholesterol, blood sugar, and body weight.

It also supplies unsaturated fats (6g unsaturated fats), which can support heart health by helping reduce LDL cholesterol, often called bad cholesterol, when they replace less healthy fats in the diet. Additionally, avocado contains potassium (250mg, 6% DV), a mineral involved in regulating blood pressure.

By providing fiber, antioxidants, healthy fats, and potassium, mango and avocado offer a convenient way to increase the nutritional value of everyday meals. However, the study did not establish whether eating the two fruits together provides greater benefits than consuming either fruit separately.

Incorporating these fruits into meals does not require a complicated eating plan. Their contrasting flavors and textures make them useful ingredients in salads, smoothies, and grain bowls.

For example, fresh mango can add sweetness to a savory dish, while avocado contributes a rich, creamy texture. Both can be used in recipes such as Mango Avocado Tuna Ceviche or an Avocado and Mango Topper.

Additional recipes and nutritional information are available at Mango.org and LoveOneToday.com.

The investigation included 82 adults between the ages of 25 and 60 who had prediabetes and were classified as having overweight or obesity (BMI 25–35 kg/m2). All participants were generally healthy, did not smoke, were not following specialized diets, and had no major chronic medical conditions.

Over eight weeks, participants followed calorie-controlled eating plans modeled on typical American dietary patterns. One group ate a medium Hass avocado and a cup of fresh mango daily, while the control group received carbohydrate-based alternatives with comparable calorie content.

To make the comparison as consistent as possible, researchers prepared and supplied meals covering 75% of each participant's estimated daily calorie needs. Participants chose their remaining foods independently, allowing some flexibility while helping the researchers limit differences between the two diets and encourage adherence.

The primary measurement was flow-mediated dilation (FMD), a noninvasive method for assessing how effectively blood vessels respond to increased circulation. Researchers also examined blood pressure, blood sugar, and other metabolic indicators, inflammation, kidney function, and dietary nutrient intake.

Despite the additional fruits, the avocado and mango group did not experience significant changes in body weight or overall calorie intake. This finding suggests that incorporating nutrient-dense foods into an otherwise balanced diet may improve certain aspects of cardiometabolic health without necessarily contributing to weight gain.

The study had several strengths, including its carefully controlled feeding approach, two parallel comparison groups, and emphasis on whole fruits rather than isolated nutrients or supplements.

However, researchers also acknowledged important limitations. The intervention lasted only eight weeks, so it remains unclear whether the improvements would persist over months or years. The participants also represented a relatively narrow population of adults with prediabetes and overweight or obesity, meaning the findings may not apply equally to people with different health conditions or dietary habits.

The research measured cardiovascular risk indicators rather than long-term outcomes such as heart attacks or strokes. Larger and longer studies will be needed to determine whether the observed changes translate into lasting reductions in cardiovascular disease risk.

Nevertheless, the findings offer an encouraging indication that relatively modest changes in food choices may benefit blood vessel health, even without weight loss or a major dietary overhaul.

This study was supported through an unrestricted grant from the National Mango Board (NMB) and the Hass Avocado Board (HAB). NMB and HAB had no role in the study design or findings.

#5655. A new tactic in the war over out-of-network bills: Health care providers are suing employers

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Herman examined hundreds of pages of court documents for this story, part of STAT’s Out of Pocket, Out of Reach series.

Bob covers the money in health care, focusing on health insurance and hospitals. His stories delve into Medicare Advantage, opaque prescription drug benefits, and how much executives actually make. He is also the author of the Health Care Inc. newsletter. You can reach Bob on Signal at bobjherman.09.

This past August, Joe Hancock, a Kentucky plumbing and heating contractor, opened a just-delivered box packed with hundreds of sheets of paper. Leafing through them, he read seven words no small business owner wants to see: “A lawsuit has been filed against you.”

The complaint, from air ambulance firm PHI Health, claimed Hancock was on the hook for almost $27,000 in medical helicopter bills. They were tied to one of his now-retired employees, who needed an emergency flight after a heart attack.

Hancock, who owns Whitehead-Hancock Plumbing, Heating & Cooling, a family-run business in Frankfort, Ky., that has been around for more than a century, didn’t understand why he was being roped into a lawsuit that featured 31 other companies — for medical charges he was never aware of.

“I was terrified,” Hancock said. “I was like, ‘What in the hell is going on here?’”

He’s not alone. The PHI lawsuit highlights an evolving tactic by health care providers in a raging battle over out-of-network bills. Previously, providers targeted health insurance companies to pay outstanding amounts that were awarded through federal mediation. Now, they increasingly are dragging the insurers’ clients — employers — into court, claiming they are responsible for bills that insurers haven’t fully paid or have delayed paying. The practice is introducing a new shock that could further torch the affordability of workers’ health coverage.

“These big suits naming dozens of employers at a time is really an escalation,” said Garrett Hohimer, a vice president at the Business Group on Health. “And it will cause employers to incur expenses that [come directly] out of their health care plans.”

A 2022 law called the No Surprises Act shielded patients from the financial trauma of many types of unexpected medical bills, but it has also given rise to a vast industry that’s driving up costs across the health care system. The law uses an arbitration process to determine how much health care providers should get paid for out-of-network emergency care, like helicopter rides, for people who have some type of commercial health coverage. STAT has reported that providers are winning most of these arbitration awards, which often are far higher than the amounts in-network providers receive for the same services.

Already, high payments tied to this process have added approximately $20 billion in extra costs to the health care system, Georgetown University researchers have estimated. A large portion of those costs inevitably come out of the bank accounts of America’s employers and consequently lead to higher premiums, emphasizing how even well-intentioned health reforms can add to the financial pressure that’s crushing workers and businesses.

PHI Health, a national chain, is arguably the most aggressive company suing employers, which it claims are not “passive” bystanders in insurers’ refusal to fully pay awards. Other regional physician practices have sued some employers as well. But PHI and its army of attorneys have filed lawsuits against hundreds of companies, demanding they collectively pay tens of millions of dollars in unpaid out-of-network claims that it won in the federal arbitration process.

PHI isn’t just suing small, local firms like Hancock’s. It’s also taking legal action against some of the largest corporations — Amazon, Walmart, Eli Lilly, United Airlines, General Motors, PepsiCo, State Farm, and Toyota, to name a few — as well as unions, counties, cities, states, public school districts, and universities.

PHI has sued other health care organizations, including hospitals, nursing homes, and medical billing firms. It also has gone after nonprofits, such as the Catholic Diocese of Cleveland. In each instance, a worker or family member at these companies took an emergency medical helicopter, often at a cost of tens of thousands of dollars per trip.

Unpacking the business — and secretive inner workings — of the U.S. health care industry

In some cases, PHI wasn’t sure what company it should be suing, but sued anyway. Several lawsuits named specific health insurers and employers as defendants, and then added “ABC CORP” or “XYZ CORP” as a placeholder. If the insurer or employer “is not in fact the plan sponsor … that covers the patient transported by PHI, then the identity of the plan sponsor is unknown to PHI, and this action is instead brought against ABC CORP,” one lawsuit reads.

Katie Keith and Ellie DeGarmo are attorneys at Georgetown’s Center for Health Policy and the Law who have tracked No Surprises Act lawsuits, including those filed by PHI. They said the scores of cases reinforce the bloat in the health care system: above-market prices that providers are winning for not participating in an insurance company’s network, attempts from insurers to not pay at all or profit off lowball offers, and a booming revenue stream for arbitrators.

But trying to wring money out of employers — and, ultimately, from their workers — is a stark divergence from the public statements of physician groups and air ambulance companies, which have painted health insurers as the bad guys for not following the rules.

“It kind of undercuts the narrative that this is provider versus insurance company,” Keith said. “In this case, this is about provider versus everyone who pays for health care and is now stuck with the bill for [arbitration] awards that have gone totally off the rails.”

STAT reached out to more than two dozen employers that were listed in PHI’s lawsuits. Most did not respond to inquiries. Of those that did, most declined to comment.

“Because this matter involves pending litigation … we will not be providing any interviews,” said Clint Mitchell, the division superintendent of Spotsylvania County Public Schools in Fredericksburg, Va. PHI Health is suing Spotsylvania County’s school system for almost $28,000.

Jay Litten, the town manager of Bridgewater, Va., told STAT the town’s health insurer, Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield, retained counsel and was handling the case. PHI sued Bridgewater in October for more than $37,000 in unpaid awards.

PHI has boasted about its success in the law’s arbitration process. In 2024, it told prospective investors that it was “able to maintain our profitability” by winning more than three out of every four arbitration claims, and it expected “this trend of favorable” outcomes from the process would continue.

The company has some private equity backing, according to financial filings from when the company considered going public in 2023. Its largest shareholder as of 2023 was Q Investments, a family office that has a private equity firm.

PHI declined to make anyone available for an interview. In a statement, CEO Scott McCarty defended the company’s lawsuits, saying the employers PHI has sued “have a duty to their employees and a responsibility to health care providers in their communities to abide by the law and pay for services delivered.”

McCarty said health insurers are asking their employer clients to choose between paying the unpaid arbitration amounts or authorizing the insurer to continue refusing payment.

“Once an employer is on notice of nonpayment and affirmatively endorses that practice, it is no longer a passive bystander,” McCarty said in the statement. “It has made a conscious decision to allow its insurance company not to pay binding federal awards in violation of federal law.”

In PHI’s lawsuits, the company alleges insurers, and now employers, are using an “unlawful scheme to ‘low pay, late pay, or no pay’ providers, including PHI.” All the cases are still pending.

The company also claims insurers float the money from unpaid awards, which are binding decisions, on the stock market as a way to earn extra interest or investment income.

James Gelfand, CEO of the ERISA Industry Committee, a lobbying group that represents large employers, said companies don’t condone insurers delaying payments as a way to make extra money. But he said under the federal law known as ERISA, employers are legally obligated to make sure they spend their health plan assets wisely on behalf of workers. If employers believe the awards are tied to ineligible claims — or are egregiously high compared with what they normally would pay — those payments could violate that obligation.

As a result, the employers’ health insurers “are operating with our blessing when we say, ‘Hey, if the [arbitration] award is inappropriate and wrong, do not pay it,’” he said. “How can we claim to be responsible stewards of people’s money if we’re just like, ‘Oh, here you go!’ That would be crazy.”

Jenny Goins, who is CEO of the National Alliance of Healthcare Purchaser Coalitions and used to oversee health benefits for Kentucky state employees, said “slow-walking the payments” to providers is one of the only ways employers can push back if they believe the awards are based on ineligible or incomplete claims. Medical claims are not eligible for arbitration if, for example, the employer or its health plan doesn’t cover a certain service or if there is certain information or data missing.

PHI has frequently named Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield, owned by Elevance Health, as a defendant in the lawsuits against employers. Elevance did not make anyone available for an interview. The company said in a statement that PHI is charging prices for air ambulance services that are 700% of what Medicare pays and mileage rates that are 1,500% more than Medicare rates.

“We have already paid PHI substantial amounts for services provided to our members,” Elevance spokesperson Janey Kiryluik said in a statement. “We dispute whether additional amounts are legally owed for claims that were ineligible” for the arbitration process.

PHI said only arbitrators can determine the eligibility of claims. It added that the rates Medicare pays don’t cover the full cost of emergency air care, nor can those prices be considered during the arbitration process.

The bigger issue revealed by the lawsuits, Goins said, is how “broken” the law has become, even though she believed it was well-intended. The issue has now attracted interest in Congress, where lawmakers are proposing various plans to overhaul the arbitration process.

“Greedy people see an opportunity to make more money,” Goins said. “I also see there’s a true opportunity to shine a light on this.”

In September, PHI dropped Hancock’s company as a defendant, one month after its attorneys served him with court papers. Hancock said his heating, cooling, and plumbing business of 30 employees is not self-insured — meaning he buys his health insurance from Anthem, which takes on all the risk of his employees’ medical care.

PHI’s McCarty blamed Anthem in a statement, saying it “does not always receive clear or consistent information from insurers identifying whether a plan is self-funded or fully insured. In this case, after the lawsuit was filed, Anthem’s counsel confirmed that Whitehead-Hancock was fully insured, and PHI promptly dismissed it, without settlement.”

Other businesses are getting released from PHI’s lawsuits, too. It’s unclear if they were wrongfully lumped in, like Hancock’s company, or if they are paying PHI’s demands to clear a costly legal headache.

PHI’s legal team “threw a handful of darts, and they’re going to try to rattle as many cages as they can,” Hancock said. “It’s not right. It shouldn’t be legal.”

STAT’s coverage of the soaring costs of health insurance for workers and employers is supported by a grant from the Commonwealth Fund. Our financial supporters are not involved in any decisions about our journalism.

Bob covers the money in health care, focusing on health insurance and hospitals. His stories delve into Medicare Advantage, opaque prescription drug benefits, and how much executives actually make. He is also the author of the Health Care Inc. newsletter. You can reach Bob on Signal at bobjherman.09.

#5654. Bella Hadid Purchases $5.5 Million ‘Enchanting Creekside Compound’ in Colorado

Supermodel Bella Hadid is Colorado-bound.

The Victoria’s Secret angel snapped up a gorgeous creekside compound in Crested Butte, CO, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Hadid, 30, purchased the three-bedroom, three-bathroom retreat for $5.5 million—a sharp decrease from its $6,995,000 asking price, set in June this year.

Listing agent Channing Boucher of LIV Sotheby’s International Realty told the publication that the daughter of the former “Real Housewives of Beverly Hills” star has already resided elsewhere in the Crested Butte area for “several months.”

In fact, she recently gushed about the state in a Nov. 9 Instagram post, shared after attending a Colorado Avalanche hockey game. Hadid posted that she's a "Colorado girl at heart" and that it "was only a matter of time before" she would find her way to the team.

It seems as if Hadid has found a perfect slice of the Centennial State to call her own.

“Tucked away on a private alley in the most desired west side of town, this enchanting creekside compound is a secret sanctuary, impossible to replicate in character or setting,” the listing boasted.

The home is nestled on a 7,841-square-foot lot with 200 feet of Coal Creek frontage. While the dwelling itself was constructed in 2001, it’s a historical property that incorporates two “original 100-year-old coal sheds,” which have been lovingly restored to serve as livable spaces.

Inside, an open floor plan features “soaring 30-foot ceilings,” and design details salvaged from century-old structures include the oversized ceilings beams sourced from a historic Columbia River warehouse, along with iron bolts and other charming items.

“The line between old and new vanish in the craftsmanship,” reads the listing, which also touts the weathered lumber used to construct the exterior and the 18th-century Virgina barn hardwood floors.

It’s easy to see why Hadid would choose the idyllic property as an escape. The listing explains that the home is in a secluded spot at the end of a dead-end gravel lane with only one other home, “free from traffic, tourists, and noise.”

The primary suite is in its own wing and constructed from a former coal shed. Skylights provide stunning views of the natural landscape, while the luxurious bathroom makes for a comfortable sanctuary.

The outdoor space is a striking complement to the intentionally designed home. It includes a creekside patio for dining and entertaining, and a soothing hot tub is located just at the edge of the water.

Though the home seems as if it exists in a world of its own, it’s not far from the vibrant attractions Crested Butte has to offer, including upscale dining and boutique shopping.

Hadid's family has been known to seek out residences that allow them to connect with nature. Mom Yolanda Hadid has a stunning Pennsylvania farm, which she previously told Realtor.com® is a place where she can “heal and reconnect with Mother Earth.”

"Eight years ago, after my divorce and years of battling chronic neurological Lyme disease, I needed to get away from the noise of city life," she explained. "I longed for a sanctuary where I could heal and reconnect with Mother Earth just the way I grew up in Holland.

"When I found the farm, I instantly fell in love. … There were no gates at that time, so I parked on the main road and walked down the long driveway; the energy was unbelievable. I instantly knew I was home even before I saw the buildings."

Yolanda listed the property for $10.88 million at the end of 2025, but pulled it off the market just three months later. However, it is understood that the delisting is temporary, and the property will most likely return to the market in the future.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5653. Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response

Children who consume more ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may have stronger brain responses to tempting foods, potentially helping explain why these products are associated with weight gain. A new study published in JAMA Network Open found that children who ate more of these foods showed heightened activity in the brain's reward system when looking at pictures of appetizing foods. Those stronger responses were also associated with increases in body fat over the following year.

Ultra-processed foods include many everyday products, such as breakfast cereals, packaged bread, and instant soups. They are manufactured to be appealing, convenient, and able to remain fresh for extended periods. Many contain artificial sweeteners, coloring agents, and other ingredients rarely used in home cooking. These products make up a substantial portion of children's diets, accounting for approximately 67% of the calories consumed by children in the United States.

Previous research has associated ultra-processed food consumption with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. However, scientists are still trying to understand the biological processes that might explain these connections. The new investigation, supported in part by the National Institutes of Health, combined magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), dietary assessments, and measurements of children's body composition to explore whether the brain's response to food could play a role.

"Children's brains are still developing, habits are still forming and food preferences are still being made. It's an important period where the brain is very sensitive to food and the food environment," said the study's senior author, Kathleen A. Page, MD, professor of medicine and pediatrics and co-chief of the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. "We're particularly interested in understanding these processes in children, because we believe that intervening early could make a real difference."

Brain Scans Reveal a Link to Future Weight Gain

To investigate these connections, the research team studied 46 children between the ages of seven and 10 who were enrolled in the ongoing BrainChild study, which examines factors contributing to diabetes and obesity. Every participant had a healthy weight when the research began, giving scientists an opportunity to investigate potential warning signs before excess weight developed.

The brain scans revealed a notable pattern. Children who consumed larger amounts of ultra-processed foods showed greater activity in the dorsal striatum when viewing food pictures. This part of the brain helps regulate reward and motivation, making it particularly relevant to how people respond to desirable foods.

Importantly, children with stronger responses in this brain region also tended to experience greater increases in BMI and body fat percentage over the next year. The findings suggest that heightened sensitivity to food cues may be one factor connecting ultra-processed diets with subsequent weight gain.

How Brain Reward Activity May Influence Body Fat

By the end of the study, children who consumed more ultra-processed foods generally had higher BMI, greater body fat percentage, and larger waist circumference.

The researchers then examined whether differences in brain activity could help account for these associations. When they adjusted their analysis to consider the children's responses in the dorsal striatum, the relationship between ultra-processed food intake and BMI became 31% weaker. The corresponding association with body fat percentage decreased by 44%.

These reductions suggest that the brain's reward response may help explain part of the relationship between ultra-processed food consumption and changes in body composition. Although the results do not demonstrate that these foods directly alter brain function, they provide a possible biological explanation for an association that has been observed in previous research.

"This study goes beyond just understanding that UPFs affect weight gain," Page said. "It actually gives us insight into the neurobiological underpinnings by which these foods may be linked to body composition over time."

The researchers caution that improving children's diets cannot depend entirely on individual families. Ultra-processed products are often inexpensive, widely available, and easy to prepare, making them practical choices for households facing financial or time constraints.

"Changing the food environment to help people access healthier, more minimally processed foods is an important part of the solution," Page said.

There are also important limitations to consider. Because the study was observational, it cannot determine whether eating ultra-processed foods directly causes heightened brain activity or increases in body weight. The findings establish relationships between these factors, but additional research is needed to determine whether one causes another.

Page hopes to address that question in a future intervention study. The proposed research would provide children who regularly consume ultra-processed foods with more minimally processed alternatives. Scientists could then examine whether changing their diets affects how their brains respond to food images and whether any differences are associated with reduced weight gain.

Meanwhile, the BrainChild study will continue tracking participants as they move through puberty and into early adulthood. By monitoring brain development, body composition, dietary patterns, and general health over time, researchers hope to gain a clearer picture of how childhood nutrition may influence long-term health.

The study was led by Page alongside Jasmin M. Alves, Ella Morgan, Brendan Angelo, Kianna Le, and Jared Smith from the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes, Department of Medicine, and Diabetes and Obesity Research Institute at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, University of Southern California. Additional contributors included Kay Jann of the USC Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, University of Southern California, and Ting Chow and Anny H. Xiang of the Department of Research and Evaluation at Kaiser Permanente Southern California in Pasadena, California.

Funding came from an American Diabetes Association Pathway Accelerator Award [1-14-ACE-36] and the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) [R01DK116858, R01DK134079]. Support for the REDCap database used in the research was provided by the Southern California Clinical and Translational Science Institute [NIH UL1TR001855].

Materials provided by Keck School of Medicine of USC. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5652. Color Health launches collabs with NCI-designated cancer centers to streamline intake

Color Health launches collabs with NCI-designated cancer centers to streamline intake" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Color Health, a virtual oncologist-led cancer clinic, has announced formal clinical collaborations with 10 National Cancer Institute-designated cancer centers.

Color and collaborating cancer centers aim to streamline time to treatment through coordinated workup (like imaging and labs) and records preparation, as well as custom intake workflows. These elements help ensure a timely start to care when weeks can be the difference between life or death, executives say. Additional partners will be announced in the coming months.

“Speed to diagnosis, speed to treatment initiation, is one of the single biggest determinants of outcomes in cancer," Caroline Savello, president of Color, told Fierce Healthcare. “Where can we make sure that there is the right clinical coordination, the right navigation coordination happening so that things can happen swiftly through the right processes."

Cancer is among the top drivers of healthcare costs and mortality. Because of its complex and variable nature, the quality and timeliness of care are the best ways to improve outcomes and manage costs. That means less duplicate testing, fewer treatment changes later and fewer avoidable ED visits and hospitalizations.

Among the collaborating centers are City of Hope-Los Angeles, Memorial Sloan Kettering, Moffitt Cancer Center, Mount Sinai, Stanford Medicine Cancer Center, UC Davis Comprehensive Cancer Center and UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center. National Cancer Institute (NCI)-designated cancer centers go through a robust evaluation for meeting quality, safety and access standards.

When care at a specific center is determined to be a good fit for a patient, Color coordinates directly to match patients with the right team, completes the clinical workup, reviews medical records and completes authorizations to each center’s specifications. First-appointment targets for most patients are set at seven days or fewer for oncology referrals placed by Color Medical. Additionally, Color verifies insurance coverage to ensure the referral is in-network. Occasionally, Color works with payers or centers on single-case agreements if something is otherwise out of network.

“Color is, above all, a very patient-centered company. When an individual faces a cancer diagnosis for the first time, Color helps to provide the information and navigation to top cancer centers. Their process balances technology with a human touch,” Karen Lu, M.D., physician in chief at Moffitt Cancer Center, told Fierce Healthcare over email.

For any patient issues, Color clinicians escalate to the collaborating centers. Patients also get ongoing wraparound support from Color during and after treatment, including nutrition, mental health, palliative and survivorship care. Additionally, Color will collaborate with the centers to identify any potential clinical trial candidates, gather the needed information and support institution-led eligibility assessment and enrollment.

UCSF Health has already worked with Color for years, so the latest collaboration is an expansion of the partnership.

“[Screening or diagnosis] can be incredibly stressful moments, and navigating a complex healthcare system should not add to that burden,” Laurel Bray-Hanin, VP at UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, told Fierce Healthcare in emailed comments. “This partnership allows us to connect Color's cancer screening and care coordination efforts directly with UCSF Health's expert patient navigators, who can help patients quickly identify and schedule the appropriate next steps.”

Color “expanded dramatically” this year, per Savello, teaming up with Independence Blue Cross and planning to serve millions more new lives in the new year through employers. Those employers continue to be laser-focused on oncology, per Savello, and are asking Color to set up partnerships with cancer centers in their regions.

“They’re all seeing, obviously, rate increases," she said. "The disease space and the market is very active."

Color partners with local providers to clinically manage all patients through its oncologist-led care team. Its virtual cancer clinic is a national center of excellence certified by the American Society of Clinical Oncology, meaning it meets rigorous standards and is subject to annual audits and reviews. The company, which started working in the cancer space in 2023, says its patients see 66% faster diagnosis and a 77% increase in screening adherence. It also claims to save $62,000 per patient in treatment and closes over three-quarters of costly care gaps.

“Cancer care isn't always a straightforward path. Sometimes, patients need answers about a possible diagnosis, and other times, they need a fresh perspective or access to new treatment options,” Bray-Hanin at UCSF said. “We want patients to feel that someone is looking out for them, helping them understand their options, and connecting them with the expertise and care they need. That commitment to providing compassionate, coordinated care is what makes this partnership so meaningful to us.”

WASHINGTON — Federal officials have granted blanket waivers to every member of an influential, yet little-known federal panel that evaluates preventive medical services, allowing them to serve despite some having clear financial stakes in decisions they might make.

The waivers, signed by a top federal official and obtained by STAT, show a willingness by health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s department to overlook financial conflicts of interests, though Kennedy frequently decries corporate influence in health care. In the case of two members, the documents show that they own private medical practices that could profit should the panel recommend particular types of care.

Other conflicts being waived include stock holdings in pharmaceutical and medical device companies and employment at public research universities that provide medical care. Some members of the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, especially the newer ones, have more extensive conflicts than others.

#5650. Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them

Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative way to turn a chemical produced by cancer cells into a weapon against them. Instead of delivering toxic drugs throughout the body, their experimental approach uses carbon monoxide released by cancer cells to manufacture anticancer compounds directly inside the cells themselves.

The research, led by Katsunori Tanaka at the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute (PRI) in Japan, was published in Nature Communications. In laboratory experiments, the team demonstrated that a specially designed compound could trigger drug production inside cancer cells without generating the same toxic substances in healthy cells. Although the technique is still at an early stage, it could eventually provide a way to attack tumors while reducing the harmful side effects associated with conventional cancer treatments.

Turning Cancer's Own Toxic Gas Against It

One of the greatest challenges in cancer treatment is destroying malignant cells without damaging healthy tissue. Traditional chemotherapy can cause serious side effects because its toxic effects are not always limited to tumors. Tanaka and other researchers are investigating more selective strategies that could make cancer treatments safer.

Their long-term goal is to replace the direct delivery of toxic drugs with relatively harmless compounds that become active only after entering cancer cells. These compounds would use substances already present inside tumors to generate therapeutic drugs exactly where they are needed.

Carbon monoxide offers an intriguing opportunity for this approach. Although best known as a poisonous gas produced by sources such as gasoline engines, carbon monoxide is also generated naturally by many types of cancer cells. Because tumors can produce unusually high amounts of the gas, it may serve as a useful biological marker for identifying cancer cells, provided it can be detected.

Scientists in RIKEN's Biofunctional Synthetic Chemistry Laboratory investigated whether they could exploit this difference. Their strategy involved delivering a metal catalyst into cells and using the excess carbon monoxide in cancer cells to drive a chemical reaction that produces a toxic compound. In principle, the reaction would occur primarily in cancer cells, where enough carbon monoxide is available, while sparing normal cells.

Protecting the Catalyst Inside Cancer Cells

To make the system work, the researchers turned to a class of compounds known as palladacycles. These metal-containing compounds can react with carbon monoxide to produce an organic molecule called phenanthridinone. Certain derivatives of phenanthridinone are toxic to cells and have already been incorporated into anticancer drugs.

However, there was a major obstacle. When palladacycles are introduced directly into cells, substances such as glutathione rapidly deactivate their central palladium catalyst. Without an active catalyst, the reaction cannot produce the desired drug.

Tanaka's team addressed this problem by building on its previous work using metal catalysts to carry out chemical reactions in living systems. The researchers enclosed a palladacycle within albumin, a protein commonly found in blood. This protective protein carrier allows the complex to travel through the bloodstream while shielding the palladium catalyst from substances that would otherwise deactivate it after entering cells.

Laboratory Tests Reveal Selective Drug Production

The scientists evaluated their system through a series of experiments. They began by testing different palladacycles to identify which one could generate the greatest amount of phenanthridinone.

Next, they exposed cultured human liver, cervical, breast, and lung cancer cells to the albumin and palladacycle complex for 48 hours. They also tested the compound on a noncancerous cell line to determine whether the same chemical reaction would occur in healthy cells.

After 48 hours, the researchers detected phenanthridinone in the cancer cell lines but not in the normal cells. The findings indicated that the albumin carrier successfully protected the catalyst from glutathione and that the chemical reaction occurred selectively in the cancer cells under the conditions tested.

The team then refined the system so that the newly formed compound could separate from the carrier and move freely throughout the cell. Additional modifications allowed the reaction to generate a particularly toxic phenanthridinone derivative already used in anticancer drugs.

When the researchers introduced this modified system into cultured liver cancer cells, they observed the anticancer compound forming inside the cells. The cells subsequently showed signs of damage caused by the toxic drug, providing proof that the approach could generate a cancer-fighting substance directly within its intended target.

Why the Experimental Drug Did Not Form in Blood

An important safety concern involved carbon monoxide already present in the bloodstream. If that gas triggered the chemical reaction before the compound reached cancer cells, the resulting drug could damage blood cells instead of its intended target.

Fortunately, laboratory testing showed that the toxic drug was not produced in blood. The researchers believe this is because carbon monoxide in the bloodstream is largely attached to hemoglobin, the protein responsible for transporting oxygen. In this bound form, the gas appears to be unavailable for the reaction needed to manufacture the drug.

The finding suggests that the system may be able to travel through blood without prematurely generating harmful substances, although further studies will be needed to establish its safety in living organisms.

"This work represents an important advance in therapeutic in vivo synthetic chemistry," says Tanaka. "In our therapeutic strategy, molecules naturally present or generated within the body -- including disease-associated metabolites -- are used as endogenous chemical feedstocks to synthesize therapeutic molecules directly at the site of disease."

The researchers now plan to move beyond cultured cells and test the approach in animal models. If future experiments are successful, the technology could help establish a new class of cancer treatments that exploit the chemistry of tumors to produce drugs directly at the disease site, potentially limiting damage to healthy tissue.

#5649. Hims & Hers reports $890.4M Q3 revenue, tightens 2026 outlook

Hims & Hers reports $890.4M Q3 revenue, tightens 2026 outlook" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Digital health and wellness company Hims & Hers tightened its full-year 2026 revenue outlook after missing Wall Street analysts’ revenue and earnings estimates.

Andrew Dudum, co-founder, chairperson and CEO, pointed investors toward the increasing scale of Hims & Hers' pharmacy and lab infrastructure. That growth is driving efficiencies for the company, as is its artificial intelligence-native experience, he said.

“That infrastructure positions us to launch treatments of increasing complexity, including testosterone replacement therapy this quarter and our Peptides Plus offering later this month,” Dudum said.

Peptides have been a focus for the company as of late, with Dudum telling investors last quarter it plans to offer already-permitted peptides, like sermorelin and NAD+.

Dudum said that Hims & Hers’ long-term strategy focuses on “three critical commitments:” being a leader in metabolic health domestically and globally, leading major markets globally and being "at the forefront of category expansion.”

“Each of these reinforces the other, and together they describe how Hims & Hers becomes the global destination for consumer health,” he said. “We are investing aggressively against all three because this opportunity is growing quickly, and we believe it will become more valuable every quarter.”

The company reported $890.4 million in revenue in Q3, up 49% compared to revenue of $599 million the year prior, according to financial results published Monday. Net loss was $33 million, compared to $15.8 million in profit for the same quarter a year ago.

Chief Financial Officer Yemi Okupe said that revenue excluded $18 million from the “scaling of membership revenue” in the company’s weight loss offering but will be recognized in the fourth quarter.

“This revenue deferral has no impact on free cash flow generation,” Okupe noted.

Adjusted EBITDA was $82.4 million compared to $78.4 million the year prior.

Ethan Feller, stock strategist at Zacks Investment Research, told Fierce Healthcare the company’s revenue was “roughly what Wall Street expected,” adding that U.S. “growth sped up to 21%.”

“But the company lost 14 cents a share against an expected gain of six cents, its third big miss in a row,” Feller said. “It is also keeping less of each sale, as gross margin fell to 57%, down from 74% a year ago, as more of the business shifts to lower-margin brand-name weight-loss drugs.”

Feller added that the company’s “growth story is still a real long-term tailwind.”

“Demand for weight-loss drugs is strong, and having both Novo and Lilly on the platform helps,” Feller said. “But as long as margins keep shrinking, the stock will likely stay under pressure until either the price falls to a level that reflects the lower margins or the company shows it can turn a steady profit.”

As a result, Hims & Hers tightened its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to a range of $3.13 billion to $3.15 billion and reduced its adjusted EBITDA guidance to a range of $257 million to $277 million.

“This is a reflection of the more aggressive strategic pricing and marketing actions that we expect to take in the U.K. and Germany, and the weight loss membership deferral noted above,” Okupe said.

The earnings report comes on the heels of an announcement that the company struck a deal with Eli Lilly to offer its branded obesity treatments directly through the Hims & Hers platform. The drugs were previously only available to patients if they left the site and went to Lilly's direct-to-consumer platform, LillyDirect.

“Nearly 3 million people across four continents rely on us to access care,” Dudum said. “That trust has made us a valuable partner to global pharmaceutical leaders like Novo and Lilly, and positions us to keep bringing the most innovative treatments to our customers as they come to market.”

Dudum added that the company is planning to launch “flexible multi-month subscriptions” across its assortment to make it easier for customers to address health goals.

#5647. Scientists solve 30-year-old mystery and discover a hidden defense against inflammation

Scientists have solved a biological mystery that remained unanswered for more than three decades, uncovering an unexpected way the immune system protects the body from its own inflammatory response. The breakthrough reveals that a chemical signal responsible for attracting immune cells to fight infections also helps prevent those same defenses from damaging healthy tissue.

The discovery came from researchers at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK), who took an unusual approach to studying inflammation. Rather than relying on mice, a standard choice for biomedical research, they turned to zebrafish. That decision helped them identify a long-mysterious enzyme and uncover a protective mechanism that had previously escaped scientists.

The findings, published October 7 in Nature, could advance research into cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and asthma. They also raise the possibility of developing treatments that strengthen the body's natural defenses against inflammatory damage.

The mystery began in 1992, when researchers at McGill University investigated a molecule that helps direct immune cells toward sites of infection. Known as 5-oxoETE, or 5-oxo-6,8,11,14-eicosatetraenoic acid, this fatty signaling molecule acts as a chemical alert when the body needs to respond to a threat.

At the time, scientists observed an enzyme that could both produce and break down 5-oxoETE. Enzymes are proteins that help chemical reactions take place, but in this case, researchers could not identify the human gene responsible for making the enzyme.

That missing genetic information created a major obstacle. Without knowing which gene produced the enzyme, scientists could not easily manipulate it in experiments or determine how problems with its activity might contribute to disease. Researchers assigned the enzyme a descriptive name based on its chemical function, but its genetic identity remained unknown for more than 30 years.

The breakthrough finally came through the work of Yanan Ma, PhD, a postdoctoral researcher at MSK's Sloan Kettering Institute. Building on earlier investigations by former lab colleague King Lam Hui, PhD, Ma identified the human gene that produces the enzyme, giving researchers a way to examine its function much more closely.

How the Immune System Can Damage Healthy Cells

Ma works in the laboratory of cell biologist Philipp Niethammer, PhD, whose research examines how cells respond to injuries, infections, and other forms of stress. His team focuses on inflammation, tissue repair, and regeneration, biological processes that also play important roles in cancer and numerous other diseases.

When harmful bacteria enter the body, chemical signals help recruit specialized white blood cells to the affected area. One of those signals is 5-oxoETE, which attracts immune cells equipped to attack invading microorganisms.

Although this response is essential for fighting infections, it carries risks. The substances immune cells release to destroy pathogens can also injure surrounding healthy tissue.

"They flood the site with toxic substances to kill the bacteria," Dr. Niethammer says. "But this can cause damage to healthy cells if it gets out of control."

Niethammer's laboratory had already spent years investigating the molecular reactions involved in 5-oxoETE signaling. Researchers were gradually identifying how the different components of the system worked together, but the unknown enzyme remained a major missing piece.

Why Zebrafish Succeeded Where Mice Could Not

Most biomedical experiments involving animals use mice or rats because their biological systems share many similarities with humans. However, these familiar laboratory animals had a significant limitation for the question Ma and her colleagues wanted to answer.

"Mice and rats are the primary model used in biomedical research," says Dr. Ma, who received a prestigious Marie-Josée Kravis WISE Fellowship in 2023 for her work on the pathway. "It makes sense -- they're mammals, and there's about an 80% overlap between their genes and ours."

Despite those similarities, mice lack a known immune cell receptor capable of recognizing 5-oxoETE. Without that receptor, researchers cannot investigate the complete signaling process in mice.

Zebrafish, however, have retained the necessary biological machinery.

"This means that you can't study the pathway in mice," Dr. Ma says. "But the pathway is intact in fish. So picking the right alternative model was critical to advancing our understanding of how the human body responds."

Using zebrafish allowed the scientists to explore how the signal operates in a living organism and eventually helped reveal a function that had gone unnoticed for decades.

Scientists Finally Identify the Missing Enzyme

Before investigating the process in zebrafish, Ma and Hui began searching for the enzyme's genetic origins using cultured human cells.

They selected several genes that might be responsible and systematically switched them off, looking for changes in the enzyme's activity. One candidate produced a decisive result.

When Ma disabled a gene called DHRS7, the enzyme stopped functioning. The experiment established that DHRS7 was the gene researchers had been searching for since the early 1990s.

Additional tests involving the rodent version of the gene showed almost no enzyme activity. That result was consistent with the absence of the 5-oxoETE receptor in mice, suggesting that rodents had lost key functions associated with this signaling system.

Identifying DHRS7 resolved the long-standing mystery. It also connected Ma's research with a separate investigation underway in the same laboratory, led by postdoctoral researcher Miklos Lengyel, MD, PhD.

"Typically, when you have a paper with two first authors like Yanan and Miklos, there is just one story that two people contributed to equally," Dr. Niethammer says. "But this paper is not like that. In this paper, there are two separate projects led by two different authors that came together as one larger discovery. And I think that's extremely important to note."

A Surprising Result Turns Expectations Upside Down

While Ma investigated the mysterious enzyme, Lengyel was using zebrafish to study colitis, an inflammatory condition affecting the colon. His experiments involved disabling selected genes to understand how they influenced intestinal inflammation.

One experiment produced an especially puzzling outcome.

Lengyel removed a gene called hcar1-4 (the zebrafish version of the human gene OXER1). This gene produces the receptor that recognizes 5-oxoETE and allows cells to respond to its signal.

Because 5-oxoETE helps attract immune cells and initiate inflammation, removing its receptor should theoretically weaken that response.

"So if you remove the receptor that detects the signal, you'd expect less inflammation, not more," Dr. Lengyel says.

Instead, the zebrafish developed intestinal inflammation on their own, even though no infection was present.

The researchers initially considered whether neutrophils, the white blood cells normally recruited by the signal, might be responsible. However, removing those immune cells did not eliminate the inflammation.

This unexpected behavior suggested that the 5-oxoETE pathway was doing something much more complicated than simply activating the immune system.

Disabling an Inflammatory Signal Makes Inflammation Worse

The connection between the two research projects became clear after Ma identified DHRS7 as the gene responsible for producing the enzyme involved in 5-oxoETE signaling.

Lengyel then disabled DHRS7 in zebrafish, preventing the production of the enzyme and disrupting the signaling process.

Based on the molecule's established role in attracting immune cells, the researchers expected inflammation to decrease. Instead, they observed the same surprising pattern seen when the receptor was removed: inflammation increased.

"It made absolutely no sense," Dr. Lengyel says. "I had to prove using several different methods before the rest of the lab was convinced."

The findings pointed to a previously unrecognized function. The signaling pathway did not simply help initiate the immune response. It also appeared to prevent unnecessary damage to healthy cells.

That dual responsibility explained why eliminating the pathway had such an unexpected effect. By disabling the system, scientists had removed not only an inflammatory signal but also an important source of cellular protection.

The Immune System's Hidden Protective Shield

Further experiments revealed how this protection works.

When immune cells attack dangerous microorganisms, they release highly reactive substances that can harm nearby healthy cells. The 5-oxoETE pathway helps tissues withstand this chemical stress, reducing the risk that the body's own defenses will cause unnecessary injury.

"This makes sense when you think about it," Dr. Niethammer says. "These immune cells unleash chemical warfare against a pathogen, and organisms have evolved an elegant way of protecting healthy cells at the same time."

The researchers found that zebrafish intestinal cells became particularly vulnerable when either 5-oxoETE or its Hcar1-4 receptor was missing. Even the normal bacteria living in the intestine produced enough low-level chemical stress to cause problems when this protective system was disabled.

The team traced the cellular protection to a group of enzymes known as NUDIX hydrolases. These enzymes help maintain cellular health by removing damaged DNA building blocks before they can interfere with normal biological processes.

Without the protective signaling pathway, intestinal cells could no longer withstand the chemical stress associated with ordinary gut bacteria. Some cells died, setting off an inflammatory response despite the absence of an invading pathogen.

The results revealed that the body uses the same molecular system both to call immune cells into action and to protect healthy tissue from the consequences.

"As it turns out, this signal isn't just an alarm, it's also a shield," Dr. Niethammer says.

Potential Implications for Cancer and Inflammatory Diseases

Understanding this protective mechanism could have important implications for diseases involving excessive or poorly controlled inflammation.

The 5-oxoETE signaling pathway is known to be disrupted in conditions such as cancer, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and asthma. By identifying its previously unknown protective role, researchers have gained a new perspective on how those disruptions might contribute to tissue damage.

In human cancers, mutations affecting DHRS7 and OXER1 (the human version of hcar1-4) have been identified in tumors of the gastrointestinal tract and uterus.

Research has also linked mutations that prevent OXER1 from functioning properly with poorer outcomes in patients with colorectal, pancreatic, and kidney cancers.

The findings suggest that strengthening the pathway might eventually help healthy tissues tolerate damaging conditions more effectively. One possible application involves protecting the intestine from oxidative stress associated with cancer treatment.

"More research is needed, but there's a possibility that activating the pathway could increase the resilience of the gut to oxidative stress -- which might help counteract damage caused by radiation therapy or chemotherapy," Dr. Lengyel says.

The discovery also has implications for diseases affecting mucosal tissues, the protective linings found in areas such as the intestines and respiratory tract.

In people with IBD, researchers have previously associated lower concentrations of 5-oxoETE in intestinal tissue with worse disease outcomes.

Evidence from asthma research points to another possible protective function. An independent study involving primates found that blocking OXER1 weakened the immune cell response but also caused protective mucus-producing cells in the airways to disappear.

Together, these observations suggest that attempts to suppress inflammation must account for the protective roles certain inflammatory signals perform. However, further research will be necessary to determine whether targeting this pathway can produce safe and effective treatments in humans.

How Physical Injury Activates the Same Defense System

The researchers are also investigating how this signaling pathway responds to physical damage, not just infection or chemical stress.

That aspect of the work is being explored by doctoral student Zaza Gelashvili, MS, who studies how cells detect mechanical forces associated with tissue injury.

When cells experience physical stress, changes to their membranes can initiate the same chain of molecular reactions involved in inflammation.

One early step occurs when stressed cell membranes release arachidonic acid, a fatty molecule that serves as the starting material for producing 5-oxoETE.

Gelashvili, a co-author of the Nature study, led a separate investigation into the molecular signals associated with physical wounds. That research was published in Nature Communications earlier in 2026. His contributions were also recognized with the 2026 Chairman's Prize from the Gerstner Sloan Kettering Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences.

"There's a mechanical component to the pathway that's upstream of what Yanan and Miklos have been studying," explains Gelashvili, a co-author on the study who led a separate study on physical wound signals that was published in Nature Communications earlier this year; his work was also recognized with the 2026 Chairman's Prize from the Gerstner Sloan Kettering Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences. "You can think of it as the first step in a chain reaction: Physical stress unlocks the raw material, oxidative stress drives the conversion, and DHRS7 amplifies the signal."

The research suggests that the body combines information about different forms of cellular stress to coordinate its response. Physical damage can initiate the process, chemical stress can influence the conversion of signaling molecules, and DHRS7 helps strengthen the resulting signal.

Rather than operating as separate responses, these processes appear to work together to help the body recognize danger while limiting unnecessary harm to healthy cells.

"What we are really studying is a pathway that integrates two completely different kinds of stress -- mechanical and metabolic -- and converts them into a single, coordinated, protective response," Dr. Niethammer says.

Additional researchers contributing to the study were Yohannes Ambaw, Leehyeon Kim, Ritchie Ly, Siyang Peng, Meysoon Quraishi, Tobias Walther, and Robert Farese Jr., all affiliated with MSK.

Financial support came from the National Institutes of Health (R35GM140883); an MSK Basic Research Innovation Award; a Starr Foundation Program for Discovery Science grant; a Tow Foundation fellowship; a Marie-Josée Kravis Women in Science Endeavor (WISE) fellowship; a Crohn's Colitis Foundation Research Fellows Award (1268111); an Experimental Immuno-Oncology Scholars fellowship; and core facility services supported in part by MSK's National Cancer Institute Cancer Center Support grant (P30CA008748).

#5643. A $35 Million Home Just Hit San Francisco’s Market, Marking the Most Expensive Listing of the Year

San Francisco’s most expensive home of the year just hit the market and is expected to draw interest from potential buyers flush with cash from the AI boom.

The home at 2770 Broadway officially went on the market on Monday with a nearly $35 million price tag.

The seven-bedroom, 6.5-bathroom home is already drawing inquiries, listing agent Neil Ward of Compass told SFGate.

Located in the exclusive Gold Coast neighborhood, the home sits on a 50-foot-wide, double-width lot, with breathtaking views of the San Francisco Bay, Golden Gate Bridge, Palace of Fine Arts, and other famed landmarks, according to the listing.

The home was designed in 1894 by Reid & Reid, the same architectural firm responsible for the iconic Fairmont Hotel. While many Gold Coast homes of this age, most of which are generational properties, need complete renovations after being sold, Ward told SFGate that the potential buyer of 2770 Broadway can “walk in with their toothbrush and their furniture.”

A 2007 renovation by architect Jim Jennings and Van Acker Construction brought together the home’s original turn-of-the-century grandeur with the functionality needed for modern family living.

The home’s 9,000 square feet are spread across four floors, where prospective buyers will find herringbone-patterned floors, arched openings, and fine millwork, all evidence of the home’s architectural greatness.

The property also features a two-car garage, wine cellar, and sport court in the rear of the house.

The home was purchased by San Francisco business executive David Chamberlain in 1989, according to SFGate. He was CEO of companies such as Shaklee, Stride Rite, and Genesco, but also had a deep connection with his city, serving as president of the San Francisco Opera and the San Francisco Chamber of Commerce.

After his death earlier this year, Chamberlain’s two daughters decided to sell the home.

Ward told SFGate that he thinks the property will sell for its $35 million asking price, which would make it the most expensive home sold on the multiple listing service in San Francisco this year.

“It is a really, really rare product that does not hit the market,” Ward said.

Between the home’s turnkey condition and the city’s competitive ultraluxury home market, Ward thinks the home’s time on the market will be brief.

“I’ve done this for over 35 years. I was here for the dot-com boom and everything in between. Nothing comes close to what’s taking place right now,” Ward said.

San Francisco is experiencing what some real estate brokerages are calling a “mansion shortage,” according to NPR. The AI boom, much of which is concentrated in San Francisco, has caused demand for luxury single-family homes in the area to skyrocket, while the supply remains stagnant.

Home to major AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, the San Francisco market had a median of just 37 days on the market, according to Realtor.com data, two weeks less than the national median of 61 days.

Some listings have had over 50 offers, and 44 homes were sold for at least $1 million over asking in June alone, according to a report from NPR.

In October, the sale of a home in San Francisco’s Presidio neighborhood broke the record for the highest sale above asking. The 1966 midcentury home was listed for $18.5 million and sold for $28.5 million, an eye-watering $10 million premium.
