#5617. A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves

Muscles can begin losing their strength and ability to recover surprisingly early in the aging process. Over time, muscle tissue may develop scar tissue, accumulate fat, and lose some of the specialized fibers responsible for rapid, powerful movements. These changes can make everyday activities more difficult and gradually reduce mobility and physical independence.

Now, scientists in Japan have identified a promising molecule that could help protect the body's natural muscle repair system and potentially make it more effective. In laboratory experiments, the compound strengthened an important biological signal involved in muscle regeneration, increasing its ability to connect with a key cellular receptor by more than twofold.

The discovery comes from a team led by Professor Ryuichi Tatsumi at Kyushu University's Faculty of Agriculture. Their findings, published in Scientific Reports, suggest a possible new approach to addressing the cellular changes that make aging muscles increasingly difficult to repair.

How Aging Disrupts the Body's Muscle Repair System

Skeletal muscles are the muscles attached to bones that allow us to walk, lift objects, maintain posture, and perform other voluntary movements. Although these muscles experience wear and tear throughout life, they also have a remarkable ability to repair themselves.

Much of that repair depends on specialized stem cells known as satellite cells. These cells normally remain inactive, positioned alongside muscle fibers until they receive a signal that repair or regeneration is needed. Once activated, they can multiply and develop into muscle cells that help restore damaged tissue.

An essential part of this process involves a protein called hepatocyte growth factor, or HGF. Despite its name, HGF plays important roles beyond the liver, including helping activate the stem cells responsible for muscle regeneration.

Under normal conditions, HGF is stored within the supportive material surrounding muscle fibers. When muscles experience an injury or mechanical stimulation, such as physical movement or stretching, the protein can be released.

HGF then attaches to a receptor called c-met on the surface of satellite cells. Receptors are specialized proteins that receive molecular signals and trigger responses inside cells. In this case, the interaction helps awaken dormant satellite cells, allowing them to multiply, mature, and participate in repairing muscle fibers.

But this carefully coordinated system becomes less reliable with age.

A Hidden Chemical Change May Weaken Aging Muscles

The researchers' previous work revealed that HGF can undergo a chemical modification known as nitration. This process attaches a chemical group called a nitro group to particular locations on a protein, potentially changing its structure and interfering with its normal activity.

For HGF, the researchers identified two especially important locations, Y198 and Y250. Both lie within the region involved in attaching to the c-met receptor.

When these sites undergo nitration, HGF becomes less capable of connecting with its receptor. The result is similar to a key that has become damaged and can no longer operate its intended lock.

This disruption could have important consequences for aging muscles. Even if the body continues producing HGF, chemical changes may prevent the protein from properly activating the stem cells needed for tissue repair. The researchers believe this mechanism may contribute to age-related muscle wasting and declining regenerative capacity.

"HGF is not necessarily missing as we age," explains Tatsumi. "Rather, it can be chemically altered after it is made. That led us to wonder whether a compound with strong antioxidant capacity might protect HGF, either by preventing nitration or by compensating for the functional loss it causes."

Scientists Test Two Powerful Sulfur Compounds

To investigate that possibility, the team studied two compounds with strong antioxidant properties: glutathione trisulfide (GSSSG) and lipoic acid trisulfide (LASSS).

Antioxidants can help limit certain types of chemical damage caused by reactive molecules. Such damage can interfere with proteins and other essential components of cells, particularly when the body's normal protective systems become less effective.

The two compounds belong to a chemical family called trisulfides. Their defining feature is a chain of three sulfur atoms connected to one another. This arrangement gives them unusual chemical properties, including an ability to participate in reactions involving the transfer of electrons, known as redox reactions.

Because these reactions play important roles in cellular chemistry, trisulfides have attracted growing interest as potential ingredients in new medicines.

In the first set of experiments, both compounds reduced nitration at the two vulnerable sites on HGF. However, preventing this chemical modification did not completely restore the protein's ability to attach to c-met.

The scientists therefore increased the amount of trisulfide used relative to HGF. They changed the molar ratio, which compares the number of molecules of each substance, from 1:4000 to 1:8000.

That adjustment produced an unexpected result.

An Unexpected Discovery Creates "Super HGF"

At the higher concentration, LASSS did much more than protect HGF from chemical damage. It also dramatically improved the protein's ability to bind to its receptor.

Compared with untreated HGF, the protein exposed to LASSS showed more than twice the binding affinity for c-met. In other words, it could attach to its target receptor much more strongly, potentially enhancing a critical step in the muscle repair process.

The treatment also made HGF more resistant to the loss of function caused by nitration, particularly at the Y198 site.

Notably, the effect was specific to LASSS. Although GSSSG had also reduced nitration in the earlier experiments, it did not produce the same improvement in receptor binding.

"This exceeded our expectations," comments Tatsumi. "We knew trisulfides had diverse biological functions, but we never expected that simply mixing HGF with LASSS would produce such a striking effect.

"What this tells us is that LASSS does more than simply neutralize reactive molecules. It may interact directly with HGF and induce a subtle structural change, creating an enhanced 'Super HGF' form that binds c-met more strongly and resists nitration."

The researchers suspect that LASSS interacts with HGF in a way that slightly alters the protein's three-dimensional shape. Because a protein's shape helps determine how well it interacts with other molecules, even a small structural adjustment could substantially change its activity.

The result is what the team describes as "Super HGF," a potentially enhanced form of the body's existing muscle repair signal.

Importantly, stronger receptor binding does not automatically establish that muscle regeneration itself has improved. Additional experiments will be needed to determine whether this molecular enhancement translates into better muscle healing and strength.

Mouse Experiments Reveal Promising Protection

After observing the effects in laboratory experiments, the researchers wanted to determine whether LASSS could also protect HGF inside living muscle tissue.

They used mice subjected to tail suspension, an established experimental method for studying muscle atrophy. By reducing normal weight bearing and muscle use, this technique produces some of the changes associated with prolonged inactivity, including muscle deterioration.

Mice that received LASSS before the experiment showed significantly less HGF nitration than untreated animals. This suggested that the compound's ability to protect the muscle repair protein was not limited to controlled laboratory conditions.

Once again, GSSSG failed to produce the same protective result.

These findings provide early evidence that LASSS can influence the chemical processes affecting HGF within living animals. However, the mouse experiments demonstrated protection against nitration, not that LASSS restored lost muscle mass or improved physical strength.

The researchers emphasize that studies involving aging animals are still necessary to establish the compound's effectiveness and safety in vivo, meaning within a living organism.

A Potential New Strategy Against Age-Related Muscle Loss

The discovery could eventually contribute to treatments aimed at maintaining muscle function during aging or extended periods of inactivity.

Muscle deterioration is not limited to older adults. It can also occur during prolonged bed rest or other situations in which muscles are used less frequently. When muscle repair mechanisms become impaired, recovering lost strength and function can become especially challenging.

Rather than replacing the body's natural repair machinery, the approach explored in this study seeks to protect and enhance an existing biological signal. If the benefits can be confirmed in future studies, strengthening HGF activity could become one strategy for supporting muscle regeneration.

The scientists also believe that the underlying effects of LASSS on HGF may extend across species. That raises the possibility of applications not only in human medicine but also in veterinary care, particularly for aging companion animals such as dogs and cats.

For now, the findings represent an early step toward understanding how a naturally occurring muscle repair pathway might be strengthened. Whether LASSS can safely and effectively preserve muscle function during aging remains an open question.

Still, the unexpected discovery that a sulfur-based compound can both protect and enhance a critical repair protein offers a promising direction for future research, with the long-term goal of helping people maintain mobility, independence, and a better quality of life as they grow older.

#5616. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5615. A compound hidden in broccoli could help fight a devastating genetic disease

A natural substance found in broccoli could offer an unexpected new approach to treating a devastating genetic disease that progressively damages the nervous system. Researchers at Swinburne University have identified promising effects from the compound, raising hopes for a more affordable and accessible treatment for patients with few available options.

The disease, known as Friedreich ataxia, causes nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord to gradually deteriorate. As the damage progresses, patients lose their ability to coordinate movements, walk, and speak. The condition can also shorten life expectancy, and there is currently no cure. Approximately 200 Australians are living with the disease.

In a new study, scientists found that sulforaphane, a naturally occurring compound in broccoli, can increase levels of frataxin, a protein that is present in insufficient amounts in people with Friedreich ataxia. The researchers also found that the compound can help protect vulnerable nerve cells from damage.

How a Broccoli Compound Could Protect Nerve Cells

Frataxin plays an important role in keeping cells functioning properly, particularly those with high energy demands, such as nerve cells. In Friedreich ataxia, a genetic defect leads to reduced production of this essential protein, contributing to the progressive damage that characterizes the disease.

Sulforaphane appears promising because its potential benefits extend beyond increasing frataxin levels. Research indicates that it can also influence several biological processes involved in disease progression, including cellular stress and inflammation. Addressing multiple sources of damage at once could make the compound a valuable candidate for further investigation.

The findings are particularly encouraging for children with Friedreich ataxia. According to lead researcher Associate Professor Faith Kwa of Swinburne University, children account for a large proportion of those affected, yet no treatments specifically approved for pediatric patients are currently available.

"Friedreich ataxia is a devastating rare genetic disease that progressively steals a child's ability to walk, speak, play, and ultimately survive," she says.

"This novel therapeutic agent can target the underlying cause of the disease, while delivering an affordable and accessible therapy worldwide, improving treatment opportunities for families affected by this life-limiting disease.

"This discovery brings us closer to a future where children with Friedreich ataxia experience a better quality of life, greater independence, and an improved chance of long-term survival."

A Potential Treatment That Could Be More Accessible

One of the most encouraging aspects of sulforaphane is that it is not an entirely unfamiliar substance. The compound already has an established safety record in both children and adults, and purified, biologically active forms are commercially available.

These advantages could make it easier to develop a widely accessible treatment if future clinical trials confirm that sulforaphane is effective against Friedreich ataxia. However, further research is essential before scientists can determine whether the promising findings will translate into meaningful benefits for patients.

Kwa explains that the rarity of Friedreich ataxia creates additional challenges for researchers. Because relatively few people have the disease, public awareness is limited, making it more difficult to attract the funding needed to investigate potential treatments.

Researchers Seek Funding for Clinical Trials

The Swinburne team hopes to secure financial support for clinical trials that would examine whether sulforaphane can deliver the same promising effects in people living with the disease.

"We are hoping to gain funding to conduct clinical trials and further prove the positive impact the broccoli compound could have on those suffering from Friedreich ataxia," she says.

"Sulforaphane already has an established safety record in children and adults, and its pure and bioactive form is commercially available. This means if clinical trials prove successful, its rollout could accelerate the path to patient impact."

For patients and families facing a progressive illness with no cure, even improvements in everyday functioning and independence could make a meaningful difference. The researchers hope their work will not only advance treatment possibilities but also bring greater attention to a condition that remains largely unknown to the public.

"Even if we can raise awareness of this debilitating condition or improve one person's quality of life, our efforts will have been worth it."

#5614. Low testosterone linked to 18% higher risk of dying from cancer

Men with very low testosterone levels may face an increased risk of developing cancer and dying from the disease later in life, according to a major international study. The findings suggest that testosterone levels could provide an early clue to future health risks, potentially years or even decades before cancer is diagnosed.

Researchers found that men with low testosterone had an 18 percent higher risk of dying from cancer. However, the relationship was not the same for every type of cancer. Surprisingly, testosterone levels were not associated with prostate cancer risk. Instead, prostate cancer was more closely linked to low levels of two other hormones, sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and luteinizing hormone.

The research comes from the Androgens In Men Study (AIMS), an international collaboration led by Professor Bu Yeap at The University of Western Australia. The project investigates how different sex hormones relate to cancer risk and other health outcomes in men.

Study Tracks Testosterone and Cancer Risk in 26,000 Men

Published in the journal Lancet Healthy Longevity, the study examined data from more than 26,000 men participating in 11 long-running studies across Australia, the United States, and Europe.

Researchers analyzed hormone concentrations in blood samples collected earlier in the men's lives. They then compared those measurements with cancer diagnoses and deaths recorded over the following decades, allowing them to investigate whether hormone levels were associated with future cancer outcomes.

The analysis included testosterone, dihydrotestosterone (DHT), SHBG, and luteinizing hormone. Luteinizing hormone is produced by the pituitary gland and signals the testes to produce testosterone.

"We wanted to know whether the concentration of these hormones in the blood was related to the risk of men being diagnosed with, or dying from, cancer into the future," Professor Yeap said.

"What we saw was that if a man had low testosterone levels - in the lowest one-fifth compared to the highest one-fifth of the range - their subsequent risk of dying from cancer was higher, even after allowing for age and other health-related factors."

Cancer Risk Increased Below a Key Testosterone Level

The researchers identified a testosterone concentration below which cancer risk began to rise. According to Professor Yeap, testosterone levels in healthy younger men typically range from 10 to 30 nanomoles per liter (nmol/L), although concentrations generally decrease with age.

Testosterone levels can also be influenced by factors that people may be able to change, including body mass index and physical activity. Certain medical conditions, such as diabetes, can affect testosterone concentrations as well.

"We saw that when baseline testosterone was below 8.6 nmol/L, subsequent cancer risk started increasing," Professor Yeap said.

"This suggests low testosterone is an important biomarker, so it's possible that looking at testosterone levels could help us identify men who might do poorly if they get cancer down the track."

These findings raise the possibility that testosterone measurements could help doctors recognize men who may face greater health risks in the future. However, the results show an association and do not establish that low testosterone itself causes cancer.

A Surprising Finding About Prostate Cancer

Because testosterone plays an important role in male reproductive health, researchers also investigated whether naturally occurring testosterone levels influenced the likelihood of developing prostate cancer.

The question has particular medical significance because lowering testosterone is an established treatment for prostate cancer. However, the new analysis found no evidence that a man's natural testosterone concentration was associated with his risk of developing the disease.

"Since reducing testosterone levels is a treatment for prostate cancer there's always been a question of whether the amount of testosterone your own body makes relates to your risk of prostate cancer but based on our findings there's no evidence they are related," Professor Yeap said.

"We did find, however, that men with low levels of SHBG and luteinizing hormone were at higher risk of prostate cancer."

The results highlight an important distinction between testosterone and other hormones involved in male reproductive function. Although low testosterone was associated with higher overall cancer risk and mortality, prostate cancer showed a different pattern of hormonal associations.

Why Low Testosterone Does Not Mean Men Need Supplements

Despite the connection between low testosterone and cancer outcomes, Professor Yeap emphasized that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation to take testosterone supplements to prevent cancer.

"While we've shown low levels are associated with increased risk, we haven't got any evidence yet that actually giving men testosterone will reduce that risk," he said.

Instead, unexpectedly low testosterone could be a reason to investigate a person's overall health. A medical evaluation may uncover underlying conditions or risk factors that require attention, even when there is no evidence of a problem affecting the testes.

"What we would say to men is if they are found for whatever reason to be low in testosterone, it's important to go to the doctor for a full checkup. It may not show any sign of testicular disease, but it might show other health issues or risk factors they need to address.

"It could be a wake-up call and encouragement for men to engage in more healthy lifestyle behaviors, and to get regular, holistic checkups to stay on top of their health."

Materials provided by University of Western Australia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5613. ‘Wake-Up Call’: Trump’s Former Housing Commissioner Says New Congress Must ‘Get Serious’ About Housing Affordability

Democrats and Republicans both understand Americans are broadly worried about the cost of living, and a former Trump administration official says it's time for both parties to take action.

In a bitterly divided Washington, DC, it remains to be seen whether lawmakers will heed that call when the 120th Congress convenes in January, with Democrats back in control of both the House and Senate.

After campaigning hard on affordability concerns, Democratic leaders say they'll use their new majorities to focus on the cost of living. Republican leaders admit they didn't heed voter concerns about the economy. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has threatened to use his veto power freely.

The summer's 21st Century Road to Housing Act, with its dozens of provisions aimed at cutting red tape, was a rare example of bipartisan consensus. What follows that landmark legislation remains an open question.

Republicans want more deregulation while Democrats aim for more support for housing. And each side must now contend with an upswell of hard-liners pushing policies that could radically change the market.

Many of the prominent names in both parties who built the housing bill are returning, including Rep. French Hill (R-AR), Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA), Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), and Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC). They're likely to return to the House and Senate committees on housing and banking.

"Now is a wake-up call," Trump's former Federal Housing Commissioner Frank Cassidy tells Realtor.com®. "Senate, House, White House. Everyone needs to get serious about tackling and addressing housing affordability. It can't be ignored anymore."

Congress had some bipartisan momentum to provide tax incentives that encourage the buying and selling of homes.

Colin Allen, executive director of the American Property Owners Alliance and a former housing issues adviser to Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC), said that could mean some ideas pitched in this Congress could come back as part of larger bills.

"They have good working relationships and have already done some bipartisan work," Allen said.

Take, for instance, the Neighborhood Homes Investment Act, which would create a new tax credit to buy and renovate homes in economically distressed areas. The bill drew 70 sponsors from both parties.

Real estate groups put in significant groundwork this year to update the capital gains tax scheme for the first time in more than 30 years. The More Homes on the Market Act came close to 200 sponsors in Congress. It would double the exclusion for many filers. It's been floating around Congress for several years and has been a target of the National Association of Realtors® and other groups.

Trump expressed some support for changing the capital gains tax scheme, though a specific plan hasn't yet materialized from the White House.

"We've done a lot of legwork to get folks behind it," Allen said. "If we're looking at a larger bipartisan bill, you can see a scenario where a few of those ideas get together. The debt limit is coming up, and there are a few other opportunities to package together."

Hill and Republicans have lobbied for more changes to the financing system. They were able to get several banking reform provisions into the Road to Housing bill. They've also floated new financial reforms to change and rescind banking rules codified in the Dodd-Frank Act and the Basel III accords after the subprime mortgage crisis. Republicans say they've chased smaller banks out of the housing market.

This summer, Hill called Dodd-Frank a "massive overreaction."

"For our smaller banks, the new regulations were a poor fit, burying them in compliance work and bureaucratic red tape," Hill said. "Instead of helping customers, their attention was diverted to filling out forms and satisfying examiners."

Mortgage reform is also a lever Congress can pull. A bipartisan group of six members of Congress pitched the First-Time Homebuyer Affordability Act this summer. It would expand access to low-interest mortgages for first-time homebuyers.

"By expanding access to financing, we can help more hardworking families achieve homeownership, strengthen our communities, and build long-term financial security," said Rep. Darin LaHood (R-IL) said.

Then there's the matter of new construction. Democrats and Republicans found some bipartisan ground in cutting some of the federal red tape that blocks construction of new homes.

Republicans also said they favor rolling back Build America Buy America provisions. Builders, they say, have complained that the sourcing requirements are time-consuming and expensive. But they've also targeted some environmental regulations that Democrats passed.

Dennis Shea, chair of the J. Ronald Terwilliger Center for Housing Policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, tells Realtor.com that some public housing authorities saw costs climb by double digits. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's waiver process is every bit as time-consuming for builders.

"A sentiment exists in both parties to change the rules, but ultimately it takes an act of Congress to exempt housing," Shea said.

Hill and other lawmakers such as Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO) have said that Congress' action should shift some burden onto states to implement reforms at the local and state level. The American Enterprise Institute said this year that state and local policy changes could boost annual homebuilding by six figures. But many of those new homes are accessory dwelling units.

Congress and the White Hose also found common ground on manufactured housing reform. All sides recognize they need to keep eyeing supply-side reforms, says Cassidy.

"Ultimately, the problem in this country is supply," Cassidy adds. "You could lower rates to 2% tomorrow, and all that will do is increase home values. It's not going to solve the underlying issue."

The other big question will be funding of the many provisions created under the Road to Housing Act. While the provisions in the bill were bipartisan, Congress must still approve funding for some of those programs. Some of those discussions are coming in the 2028 fiscal budget and beyond.

Over the months of negotiations on the Road to Housing bill, some Republicans took issue with unfunded mandates in it. Concerns about funding programs, and at what level, could spill over into congressional proceedings in coming years.

Tony Marquez, director of American University's real estate program, who has a long career in real estate and banking, tells Realtor.com that the industry is still amenable to a few different ideas for how to solve housing. It doesn't rely on one side's control of the government.

"My un-professional assessment is we'll have a certain amount of gridlock over a number of years where Democrats may come up with some suggestions," Marquez says. "But the answer to affordable housing is not just one silver bullet. It can have many elements."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5612. Staera launches with $4.6M to develop an optical interconnect for chiplets

Staera Semiconductor Inc., a startup that develops technology for linking together chiplets, launched today with $4.6 million in pre-seed funding.

Singaporean fund Openspace Capital led the investment. It was joined by SGInnovate, Black Kite Capital, 28 Holdings, In Group and financial software company Decimus Technologies.

High-end artificial intelligence accelerators comprise multiple chiplets, silicon dies that each perform a narrow set of tasks. They’re linked together by a kind of miniature network that also functions as the host accelerator’s base layer.

That miniature network takes the form of an interposer, an advanced device that sometimes includes computing circuits, or a bridge. A bridge is essentially a small interposer that costs less to make.

Interposers and bridges both use tiny copper wires to move data between the chiplets they connect. San Francisco-based Staera hopes to replace those copper wires with optical links. According to the company, optical technology is faster and uses less power. It can also transmit data over longer distances without slowing down, which enables chipmakers to build bigger accelerators.

“Copper performance plummets over the millimeter-to-meter distances that matter most in AI accelerators, and bolt-on optics add power and complexity.” said Chief Executive Officer Andrew Kim. “We build the light into the chip, the entire optical link inside a chip, so the connection gets smaller, cooler and faster with each generation.”

Staera’s first product is called Lightwire. It transmits data over optical links, or waveguides, made of a transparent material known as silicon nitride. Light beams can only travel through a transparent material if their wavelengths fall within a specific range. Silicon nitride supports a larger range of wavelengths than many alternatives and causes less light loss, which boosts connection speeds.

The light beams into which Lightwire encodes data traffic are produced by miniature LEDs. Those devices are made of gallium nitride, a compound that is widely used in optical systems because it has a direct bandgap.

The electrons that orbit an atomic nucleus have different energy levels known as bands. Light is produced when an electron jumps from one band to one another and then collides with a quasiparticle called an electron hole.

Usually, the process also involves a second quasiparticle known as a phonon. Direct bandgap materials such as gallium nitride don’t require a phonon, which makes the light generation process more efficient.

Staera says Lightwire transmits data between an AI accelerator’s chiplets at a rate of up to 8 gigabits per second. The technology can provide more than 600 optical links per square millimeter. In practice, that means a Lightwire-powered HBM4 memory stack can move up to 24 terabits of data per second instead of the 2.8 terabits supported by current technologies.

Staera’s funding round will advance its commercialization efforts. It will enhance Lightwire, grow its U.S. team and build out a manufacturing supply chain. The company hopes to begin commercial shipments in 2030.

#5611. Patrick and Brittany Mahomes Are Expecting Baby No. 4—Inside the Custom Missouri Mansion Where They’re Raising Their Growing Family

Patrick and Brittany Mahomes are expecting their fourth child, and the newest member of the family will have plenty of room to play at their custom-built Missouri mansion.

The Kansas City Chiefs quarterback and his wife, both 31, took to Instagram to share the joyous news that their family is expanding.

"Another blessing from God....& then there were 6," they captioned an image of them and their three kids, Sterling Skye, 5; Golden Raye, 1; and son Patrick "Bronze" Lavon Mahomes III, 3, on a beach.

The couple's growing family means one more child will get to turn their at-home, indoor basketball court into a playground.

The couple's extraordinary property sits on a huge 8-acre parcel they snapped up for just $400,000; however, the dwelling that now occupies it is understood to be worth millions more.

Images have revealed that the home features a stunning swimming pool, complete with its own water slide, as well as a large sports field that has "Mahomes" written across one end.

And Patrick isn't restricting himself to just football as far as his at-home sporting amenities go. In addition to the field, he and Brittany added a putting green and a private pond.

In October 2024, the home was the site of a burglary, an incident that he later described as "frustrating" and "disappointing."

Patrick and his wife are believed to have moved into their home in 2023, having spent close to three years completing their dream abode. At around the same time, they also listed their former Kansas City dwelling—a much more modest house they purchased in 2019.

According to local regulations, home sale prices do not have to be disclosed, meaning that the final sale price is not known. However, they put the abode on the market for $2.9 million. Before the couple purchased the property, it was last listed for $1.99 million.

The expectant mom of four previously shared a very candid glimpse inside the couple's lives at home with their three children, shedding a very entertaining light on the chaos that erupts when the kids are allowed to run loose around the upscale abode.

In a video posted to her Instagram Stories, the entrepreneur and fitness trainer revealed the havoc that her kids had caused inside Patrick's private at-home basketball court, which has, for all intents and purposes, been turned into a makeshift playground.

The clips showed the couple's children crawling around in the space, before panning the camera to reveal the court surface was covered in an array of toys, as well as two bounce houses.

Adding insult to injury, Brittany poked fun at her husband for daring to think that the basketball court would be one space inside the home that he could call his own, saying: "I really think it's hilarious that Patrick wanted this basketball court because he thought it was going to be his."

In the first clip, two of the kids could be seen playing on the ground in front of a "Spider-Man"-themed bounce house—with Patrick III sporting a superhero costume in honor of the Marvel favorite.

His younger sister, meanwhile, holds what appears to be a pickleball racket in her hand as she walks toward her sibling.

As Brittany pans the camera around the room, dozens of other toys are seen littered across the floor—from scooters and ride-on bikes to pink ponies, several of which are covering the NFL quarterback's custom "MAHOMES" logo that runs along one side of the court.

It looks as though the court had, at one point, been set up for all manner of sporting events; a rack of fresh basketballs sits to one side, while a tennis net has been set up on the center line.

But the chaos did not end with the basketball center—with Brittany later revealing that the kids kept the fun going even after they made their way upstairs, where she was greeted by a trail of "Spider-Man" costume pieces laying in a trail on the floor.

“The trail of a kid that had to poop,” she joked.

Despite Brittany joking about their kids taking over the basketball court, Patrick did previously reveal when they were building the house that he had always intended for the space to be "for the kids."

"I’m going to have a half-football field so I can get some work in with some guys out there," he shared during a 2021 interview with NBC Sports. "I’ll have a basketball court ... [but] that’s not for me, that’s for the kids. It’ll have a little golf stuff out there as well."

Then, in 2023, he and Brittany transformed the basketball court into an indoor football stadium in honor of Bronze's first birthday, complete with balloon displays and custom bounce houses for the kids to enjoy.

Luckily, the basketball court is far from the only space inside the palatial property where Patrick can enjoy some peace and quiet at his home, which boasts incredible amenities, both inside and out.

In addition to that primary residence, the couple also owns a vacation home in Texas, where they first met.

The four-bedroom, 7,800-square-foot estate on a half-acre lot comes with lots of baller perks: a wine room, family room with a gas fireplace, and an outdoor space with a gas fireplace, grill grotto, firepit lounge area, large pool, tan deck, and spa.

#5610. The next chapter for Red Hat: AI agents rewrite the cloud-native playbook

Red Hat LLC has spent years making Kubernetes manageable for enterprises that would rather run applications than tend clusters. As AI agents move into production, the company is extending that experience to a new generation of workloads. AI agents don’t just consume infrastructure. They execute commands, call external tools, access enterprise systems and take actions that can affect the business. The next phase of AI agent infrastructure requires enforceable security boundaries alongside efficient resource management.

Red Hat arrives at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City this week with a growing portfolio of technologies addressing those requirements. OpenShift provides the Kubernetes foundation; its work with Nvidia Corp. on OpenShell addresses agent execution and security; and the llm-d project has reached version 1.0 with capabilities for serving the context-heavy workloads agents create. Together, these developments position Red Hat to help enterprises manage agentic AI through open, Kubernetes-based infrastructure.

Unlike conventional applications, autonomous agents can generate commands, invoke tools and delegate work across multiple systems. That flexibility creates opportunities for automation while increasing the importance of consistent access controls and oversight.

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of how cloud-native infrastructure is evolving to support enterprise AI, with Red Hat and the broader Kubernetes ecosystem addressing the security, operational efficiency and scalability requirements of autonomous agents. (* Disclosure below.)

The rapid adoption of OpenClaw has brought renewed attention to agent security. An agent that can read files, run shell commands and make network calls needs clearly defined permissions and isolation to operate safely within enterprise environments.

Red Hat’s response centers on its collaboration with Nvidia around OpenShell, a runtime that places agents inside isolated execution environments and applies policy to their access. Nvidia developed OpenShell; Red Hat is working with Nvidia and the wider community to integrate the technology into Red Hat AI and its open hybrid cloud platform. Red Hat’s announcement describes the work as part of a broader effort to bring security-focused agentic AI capabilities to enterprise infrastructure.

OpenShell uses sandboxing, process-aware policy and controls over network access and credentials. Red Hat has also described how OpenShell can work with OpenShift’s sandboxed containers, adding application-level restrictions inside a virtual-machine boundary. These complementary layers govern agent behavior and isolate the environments in which agents operate, as Red Hat explains in its technical overview of layered sandboxing.

The distinction matters because sandboxing does not make an agent trustworthy. It limits the damage an agent can cause when its instructions, generated code or external inputs lead it somewhere they should not.

In a recent interview with theCUBE, Pete Cheslock, principal AI community architect at Red Hat, described how OpenShell builds on Kubernetes infrastructure: “The agent sandbox is one of them, so that you can deploy these agents in a secure way using Kubernetes native APIs.” His comments get to the central issue: enterprises cannot delegate authority to agents without defining and enforcing its limits.

Red Hat Chief Technology Officer Chris Wright also emphasized the importance of agent isolation in a May interview with theCUBE. Agents that can take real actions in a business need sandboxing and least-privilege protections, he explained.

“You’ve got to give it the right sandboxing. You’ve got to put protections around the agent, give it least privileges so it doesn’t think about read versus read-write — very big difference,” Wright said in SiliconANGLE’s coverage of Red Hat Summit.

Beyond sandboxing, enterprises must manage agent identities, data permissions, tool access and authorization. That distinction is reinforced by Paul Nashawaty, practice lead and principal analyst for application development, modernization and cloud native at theCUBE Research, whose September analysis of AI agent governance examines the difference between observing what agents do and proving what they were authorized to do. The research identifies runtime enforcement, delegated authority and verifiable audit evidence as requirements that become more important as autonomous systems move into production.

“This creates an opportunity for platforms that can unify application development, infrastructure orchestration, security and observability rather than adding another layer of disconnected tooling,” Nashawaty said.

Beyond security, agents create new requirements for inference infrastructure. An agent may call a model, retrieve information, invoke a tool and return to the model with additional context. Each interaction consumes compute, memory and network capacity, while the system must preserve enough context to continue efficiently.

Red Hat’s llm-d project addresses part of that problem. Founded by Red Hat, IBM Corp., Google Cloud, CoreWeave Inc. and Nvidia, and now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, llm-d uses Kubernetes-native components to distribute inference across accelerators and manage traffic between them.

The project reached version 1.0 on Oct. 20, adding session-aware routing, turn-priority scheduling, multi-tenant quality-of-service controls and high-availability operations. Those features aim to keep multi-turn requests close to cached context, prioritize latency-sensitive work and reduce disruption during maintenance. The Red Hat release announcement and Google Cloud’s technical overview describe the release.

The architecture provides operators with additional options for coordinating inference workloads and managing accelerator resources within Kubernetes.

Red Hat Senior Vice President and AI Chief Technology Officer Brian Stevens described one of llm-d’s central architectural decisions in SiliconANGLE’s report on Kubernetes inference: “We can independently scale the processing of the input from the production of the tokens.”

Other infrastructure providers are addressing complementary requirements. ScaleOps Labs Ltd. focuses on GPU utilization and resource optimization across Kubernetes workloads. Vultr Holdings LLC offers GPU infrastructure and Kubernetes-based model deployment, while Broadcom Inc. positions VMware Cloud Foundation as a private-cloud platform for Kubernetes and AI workloads. Together, these offerings reflect expanding enterprise choices for resource optimization, accelerator capacity and private-cloud operations.

The operational gap appears in theCUBE Research’s “Day 0 Build, Test Survey Research Report.” Based on a survey of 375 IT, development, operations and platform engineering professionals, the research found that cloud-native adoption is widespread but maturity remains uneven. Inconsistent automated testing, fragmented developer tools and gaps in rollback capabilities continue to complicate production deployment.

“Ninety-two percent of organizations are integrating AI into at least one stage of the software development lifecycle, while 79% expect full-scale AI agent adoption within the next three years,” Nashawaty said, adding that approximately 30% still face operational readiness challenges.

The broader industry is also moving toward production-scale infrastructure. The CNCF’s 2026 annual cloud-native survey found that 82% of container users run Kubernetes in production and that 66% of organizations hosting generative AI workloads use Kubernetes for some or all inference. Those figures reinforce Kubernetes’ expanding role as enterprises adopt AI workloads.

The open-source ecosystem is expanding alongside agentic AI adoption. On Nov. 5, Google announced the donation of Agent Substrate, gVisor and OpenRL to the CNCF following their acceptance into its Sandbox program in October. The projects address agent execution, isolation and reinforcement-learning workflows. Agent Substrate separates agent sessions and identities from active compute, allowing idle environments to pause and resume; gVisor provides an additional isolation boundary for untrusted code; and OpenRL supports reinforcement-learning post-training on Kubernetes. Google’s announcement describes the projects and their transition into CNCF governance.

These contributions complement broader efforts across the Kubernetes community. Red Hat is a co-founder of llm-d and is integrating Nvidia’s OpenShell into its enterprise AI platform, while Google is contributing technologies related to runtime and training requirements. The common emphasis on open infrastructure creates opportunities for interoperability as enterprise AI systems mature.

Broadcom added another development on Nov. 9, announcing that its VM API project had been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox. The project aims to let organizations manage virtual machines through Kubernetes application programming interfaces across different infrastructure providers. This extends the Kubernetes conversation to managing virtual machines alongside containerized workloads.

Project Lightwell adds another dimension to Red Hat’s enterprise strategy. Announced with IBM in May, the $5 billion initiative aims to use AI-assisted vulnerability identification and validated fixes to strengthen open-source software supply chains. The initiative extends security efforts to the software dependencies supporting production workloads.

Sam Weston, industry analyst for enterprise applications, development and modernization at theCUBE Research, points to the infrastructure mix enterprises already operate.

“With our data showing 61.8% of enterprises run hybrid deployments and an additional 10% operate across multi-cloud environments, Red Hat’s hybrid-first platform strategy aligns closely with where enterprise infrastructure lives today,” Weston said.

Red Hat’s established OpenShift footprint provides a foundation for connecting these developments. As enterprises deploy more autonomous workloads, the company is positioned to combine Kubernetes orchestration, agent isolation and distributed inference within its broader hybrid cloud strategy.

The opportunity extends beyond any individual project. OpenShift, llm-d and OpenShell illustrate how Red Hat is contributing to an open infrastructure model that accommodates both conventional applications and emerging AI agents.

For enterprises, the objective is to make AI workloads secure, efficient and manageable without losing control over how autonomous systems operate. Red Hat’s work across the Kubernetes ecosystem reflects how that foundation is taking shape.

#5609. Homebuilders in Fire-Ravaged Altadena Are Using 3D Printing To Rebuild

Residents walking through Altadena, CA, recently were struck by an odd sight this week: A large gantry crane appeared to be "printing" out 11-inch-thick concrete pillars and walls.

The robotic 3D-printed machine, designed by Dutch company COBOD, was being used to rebuild a home that had been destroyed by the Eaton Fire in January 2025, extruding layer after layer of concrete and shaping it into walls.

The home is a project of Emergent Home, a Los Angeles-based builder that's been contracted to produce seven concrete-printed homes in Altadena.

Emergent was actually founded in 2019 to help rebuild after the Carr Fire destroyed more than a thousand homes in Northern California.

3D-printed concrete has gained attention in recent years because of its sturdiness and cost effectiveness—especially in fire-prone areas. The precise nature of the process reduces construction waste and completion time. According to COBOD, homes can be completed twice as fast as conventional construction and at up to 30% less than conventionally built homes.

Most importantly, the homes are fire resistant.

The January 2025 Eaton wildfire ravaged more than 14,000 acres and destroyed more than 6,000 homes. Yet despite the numerous fires and climate risks, the vast majority of homes in the area continue to be constructed with wood.

"Ninety-five percent of this community is rebuilding with wood," Ken Calligar, the CEO of building technology company RSG-3D, previously told Realtor.com®. "It's insane."

"A 6-year-old could have said this wasn't a good idea," he continued. "These towns are so vulnerable, they have no idea. To me, it's so obvious what the solution is."

RSG-3D builds with framing panels made of steel wire and expanded polystyrene wrapped in concrete skins—and is somewhat different from the 3D printed concrete Emergent Construction is using.

The share of 3D-printed concrete homes in the U.S. remains relatively small. So far only a couple hundred homes have been built using the technology. But proponents believe that as climate disasters continue to plague homeowners, and as costs continue to hobble the building industry, the technology will grow in popularity.

Already, one homeowner is getting ready to move into her 3D-printed concrete home. In September, PCI Builders collaborated with RIC Robotics and Stone River Dynamics to produce the first permit-approved 3D-printed concrete house in the area.

The home was for Cindy Lopez, an Altadena resident whose home burned to the ground on Jan. 8, 2025.

“This home represents more than my own recovery, I hope it helps other families see what is possible while encouraging local governments to recognize and invest in 3D-concrete printing as a meaningful option for communities facing increasing wildfire risk," Lopez said in a statement.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5608. Why Builders May Be More Motivated To Sell Than Homeowners

Here’s something most homebuyers don’t think about. When the housing market slows down, homeowners and builders don’t always respond the same way.

Think about it. If you’re selling your house and aren’t getting the offers you want, you could make the choice to take it off the market and stay put, and wait for things to improve.

But builders? They may be more motivated to stay the course.

They’ve already invested money in building those houses. And every completed home that sits unsold means money tied up in a property, plus ongoing costs that can add up.

That’s why some builders may be more motivated to negotiate right now. And that could work in your favor.

You’ve probably seen the headlines. According to the latest report from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), pending home sales – homes that have gone under contract but haven’t closed yet – fell 7.3% in September and 11.3% compared to last year.

Why? Higher mortgage rates are making it harder for buyers to make the numbers work. Now, that report tracks existing homes, not new construction. But we’re seeing signs of the same slowdown on the builder side, too.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), builder confidence dropped to 29 in October, its lowest level since June 2012. Traffic from prospective buyers also dropped to its lowest level in more than a decade, excluding the start of the pandemic.

As Robert Dietz, Chief Economist at NAHB, explains:

“Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines.”

A homeowner may be able to wait for the right offer. But a builder with several finished houses sitting unsold may have more reason to get those homes sold sooner rather than later.

And that means they may be more willing to work with you than you think.

If you’ve always assumed builders don’t negotiate, take a look at what they’re actually doing. According to the latest survey from NAHB, in October:

65% of builders are offering sales incentives.

43% are cutting prices, the highest share recorded between 2020 and 2026.

And 6% is what they’re typically taking off the price.

So, yes. Builders absolutely do negotiate. And with demand slowing, there’s good reason to explore just how flexible they may be right now.

That could mean asking for a lower price. But it could also mean asking for a mortgage-rate buydown, help with closing costs, or upgrades that would otherwise cost you extra.

And here’s a tip that could make a real difference.

Don’t just look at the newest communities or the prettiest model homes. Look for builders with completed houses that haven’t sold yet.

Those are sometimes called quick move-in homes or spec homes. And the longer one of those move-in ready homes sits unsold, the more reason a builder may have to consider an offer that helps get it off their books.

Don’t assume the advertised price or incentive package is the best they’ll do.

This is where having your own agent can really pay off. An agent who knows the local market can help you compare what builders are offering, identify communities with more available homes, and understand where there’s room to negotiate.

Of course, not every builder will offer the same incentives. And some may be more flexible on closing costs or mortgage rates than on the price itself.

The trick is knowing where to look, what to ask for, and how much room there may be to negotiate. And that’s where having your own agent is key.

A homeowner who isn't ready to accept a lower offer may be able to wait. But a builder with finished houses to sell has a different set of priorities. And that could work in your favor.If you're ready to buy, talk to a local agent about which builders have completed homes sitting on the market in your area see what they're willing to offer to get them sold.

#5607. Flashpoint launches threat investigation AI agents to automate security work

Threat intelligence company Flashpoint today introduced Flashpoint Agentic AI, a new product that provides purpose-built artificial intelligence agents to help organizations accelerate threat investigations, automate cybersecurity intelligence tasks and scale operations.

Today’s threat environment is increasingly fueled by AI, which has brought the bar down considerably and allowed malicious actors to scale their operations. AI is transforming cyberattacks by making them faster to develop, more scalable, cheaper to execute and more difficult to detect. This means that any time a new vulnerability is uncovered, it can be exploited in record time.

Individuals with little or no knowledge of programming or infrastructure can use large language models to rapidly develop attack patterns, write malicious code and plan attack paths.

“The AI threat landscape is accelerating faster than many threat intelligence teams can keep up,” said founder and Chief Executive Josh Lefkowitz. “Flashpoint Agentic AI helps close that gap by taking on recurring work that unnecessarily consumes teams’ time, freeing them to focus on connecting the dots.”

As part of the new offering, the company is launching Agentic Hub, a new environment within Flashpoint Ignite, a cyberthreat intelligence and vulnerability management platform, that brings together chat and purpose-built agents, along with product-specific agents.

The company said that instead of traditional AI agents, which support individual tasks such as search and summarization, the new Agentic AI product allows teams to delegate defined, multi-step intelligence work to specialized agents.

Agent Hub will initially launch with chat that can turn any question into a multi-step investigation, follow the traces of vulnerability, credential, fraud and threat actor intelligence to provide source-linked information. A series of agents provides intelligence briefings, alert setup and triage. Finally, the PIR Agent takes plain-language intelligence requirements and turns them into structured PIRs, or priority intelligence requirements, that provide specific, decision-oriented guides for an organization to collect and analyze cyber threat intelligence.

According to the company’s 2026 Enterprise Threat Intelligence Report, 65% of survey respondents identified alert noise and false positives as a challenge affecting security effectiveness, while 55% cited insufficient analyst bandwidth.

#5606. Who’s Buying Homes with Cash Right Now?

Ryan Serhant, CEO of SERHANT, says there isn’t just 1 housing market right now. There are really 4: cash buyers, buyers who need a mortgage, homeowners with low mortgage rates, and builders.

Today, let’s zoom in on the 1st group – cash buyers.

According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR), 27% of homes sold in September were bought with all cash. That’s more than 1 in 4 buyers. And that’s a pretty big number, especially when so many people are struggling with affordability.

So where is all that cash coming from? When you hear a number like that, it’s easy to picture wealthy investors buying up houses left and right. But that’s not necessarily the case. Some of those cash buyers are actually homeowners who’ve built up enough equity to buy their next home outright.

Here’s what you should know about who’s paying cash and what that really means for the market.

Cash buyers tend to fall into a few groups, according to NAR:

Homeowners who sold a house and are using that money to buy their next one

So, it’s not all those big investors social media talks about. That 1st group may include people a lot more like you. Here’s how. According to Cotality, the average homeowner with a mortgage has about $310,000 in equity.

That’s a big deal right now. Many homeowners feel stuck because they don’t want to give up the low mortgage rate they have today. But once they learn they may have enough equity to move and pay cash for their next home, today’s rates don’t matter nearly as much. Because buying in all cash means…

No need to borrow at today’s mortgage rates

No loan approval process, so you may be able to close faster

And even if the equity won’t cover the whole purchase, putting more of it toward the next home means borrowing less. That can mean a smaller monthly payment, too.

But cash buyers like this are more common in some places than others. And how big of a segment of your local market this is, is going to depend on where you live.

For example, Realtor.com data shows cash buyers made up almost 47% of sales in Mississippi and 46% in Montana earlier this year (see map below).

According to Realtor.com, the states with the most cash buyers reflect “a mix of affordability, wealth and buyer demographics.” Think places with lower home prices, or lots of retirees and 2nd-home buyers.

So, depending on where you live, you may see a lot more (or a lot fewer) cash buyers than the national number suggests. An agent who knows your area can tell you who’s actually buying near you.

And if all of this has you thinking everyone’s paying cash, they’re not. If you’re planning to buy and need a mortgage, you’re actually in the majority.

Based on NAR’s numbers, nearly 3 out of 4 home purchases still involve financing. And for homes priced between $200,000 and $750,000, only about 1 in 5 sold for cash, according to Realtor.com (see graph below):

That means most people buying in that price range are financing their purchase, too. So, there’s no need to assume you’re at a disadvantage just because you’re using a loan.

So, what does all this mean for you? Maybe more than you think.

If you already own a house, you may have enough equity to make your next move more affordable than you realize. And if you’re buying with a mortgage, remember, you’re in good company. Most buyers are financing their purchases, too.

The takeaway? Don’t make assumptions about what’s possible based on how other people are buying homes. What really matters is your equity, your budget, and what’s happening in your local market.

Cash buyers are a meaningful part of today’s market, but they aren’t the whole market.Whether you’re hoping to put your equity to work or you’re buying with a mortgage, a local real estate agent can help you see how much equity you have, who’s buying in your area, and what that means for your next move.

Cash buyers are a meaningful part of today’s market, but they aren’t the whole market.

Whether you’re hoping to put your equity to work or you’re buying with a mortgage, a local real estate agent can help you see how much equity you have, who’s buying in your area, and what that means for your next move.

#5605. Alix Earle’s Feud With Alex Cooper Resurfaces—Inside Her Family’s $4.1 Million New Jersey Home Where She Told Her Side

Social media sensation Alix Earle’s falling-out with Alex Cooper is back in the spotlight after Sofia Franklyn revisited her own split from the “Call Her Daddy” co-founder in her new explosive memoir, "Daddy Issues."

Earle, 25, previously pulled back the curtain on her side of the story from inside her family’s $4.1 million New Jersey home, where Netflix’s "Earle Meets World" cameras captured how the feud took an emotional toll on her.

Now, that drama has been brought to a boiling point after Franklyn shared her own experience with Cooper, 32, in her tell-all book, detailing the experience that took the once-co-hosts from friends to enemies.

Following the release of her book, Earle made it clear whose side she was on when she shared a TikTok video of her reading Franklyn's memoir.

Earle and Cooper were once known to share a close friendship, but their relationship appeared to sour after Cooper dropped Earle's podcast, "Hot Mess," from her Unwell Network in early 2025, sparking rumors that a feud had erupted between the two.

After Earle was publicly seen liking negative comments about Cooper on social media, the latter posted a video urging her online nemesis to air her grievances in public.

Earle responded to Cooper's video with a brief, "On it," but stopped short of sharing her side of the story at the time. Instead, she later teased that fans would finally get answers about what happened between the pair in the Netflix series.

"She's trying to paint it as I'm just like this crazy lunatic who is hating her for no reason. There's a reason," Earle said.

In her Netflix series, Earle opened up about the drama with Cooper, telling her family, “From the start, I didn’t realize things were going wrong because I was obsessed with her. I was like, ‘This is my idol. I’m so happy to work with her,’ and then [I] constantly felt taken advantage of and used and mistreated and manipulated.”

Holding back tears, she said, “What I was thinking—which makes me so sad for me at the time—is I was so happy. I trusted her so much, and all she did was just s--- on it.”

She explained, "We’re filming her podcast, and she’s having us drink before and then asking me really sexual questions I wasn’t comfortable with. But then I’m also answering ‘cause I’m drunk. I’m imagining myself in her shoes, to take someone in college, who’s young, impressionable, you know looks up to you, and then ask them these raunchy questions. It’s stuff that I didn’t necessarily want to live on the internet forever.”

The series, which hit screens on Sept. 4, also offered fans the the most revealing look yet at the behind-the-scenes drama that will be played out on screen for the world to see, including the difficult relationship between Earle's mother, Alisa, and her stepmother, Ashley Dupré, as well as the TikTok star's split from NFL player Braxton Berrios.

"Earle Meets World" take fans inside the star's world as she navigates her booming career, complicated relationships, family dynamics, and the hardships that come with being in the spotlight.

And while Earle has become known for documenting everything from her nights out to her acne struggles, with her millions of followers, the series promises to offer a much more intimate look at what happens when the cameras—or, in her case, the phone—would normally stop rolling.

"There's so much more to my life that people don't get to see,” Earle admitted in the trailer.

The reality series also brings Earle's family firmly into the spotlight, giving viewers a glimpse at the people closest to the influencer as she attempts to balance her increasingly high-profile career with her personal life.

"Every time I step out, there's a story," Earle lamented in the clip.

And among the familiar faces featured in the series is another backdrop that longtime Earle followers may recognize: her family's sprawling New Jersey mansion.

Earle's father and manager, Thomas "TJ" Earle, and her stepmother purchased the property in 2013 for $2.25 million, property records previously reviewed by Realtor.com® reveal.

The pair scored quite the deal on the home, which had previously been listed for $3.35 million. Today, the dwelling is estimated to be worth around $4.1 million, according to Realtor.com.

TJ and Ashley share the home with their three children, Izabel, Penelope, and Thomas, while Alix and her sister, Ashtin Earle, regularly return to New Jersey to spend time with their family.

Over the years, Alix has offered her millions of social media followers glimpses inside the property, revealing that the family has made numerous changes to the dwelling since purchasing it.

Now, the home is poised to serve as one of the backdrops for the family's next chapter as Netflix cameras capture the highs and lows of their lives for Earle's first reality series.

"My family is full of chaos," Earle said in the trailer.

In addition to putting Earle's close-knit blended family front and center, the show will also highlight the TikTok's romantic life, specifically her relationship with former boyfriend and NFL star, Berrios.

In one scene of the trailer, Earle's family can be heard confessing that they are "team Braxton." It then cuts to a clip of the social media icon crying as she admits she struggled to balance both her "break up" as well as the news of her mom's cancer diagnosis—both of which occurred while she was filming "Dancing With the Stars."

Earle's mother, Alisa, can also be seen opening up about the complicated relationship she shares with Dupré, telling the camera: "I'm side by side with someone who had an affair with my husband. You don't forget what happened. It doesn't mean we can't enjoy the people that we love."

Ashtin can then be seen telling her family members that they have "such a special dynamic."

The series also documents the enormous changes that have taken place in the influencer's own life since she first found fame filming "Get Ready With Me" videos from her student housing at the University of Miami.

Since graduating in 2023, Earle has transformed her enormous online following into a sprawling career, complete with lucrative brand partnerships, red-carpet appearances, and business ventures.

"I started sharing a more unfiltered look into my life, and then it just amped up," Earle says in the teaser.

But “Earle Meets World” promises to go beyond the polished snapshots of that success, documenting the more complicated reality of navigating fame, family, friendships, and relationships while millions of people watch.

Earle's sister Ashtin will feature prominently alongside her, as well as several of Earle's close friends.

While Earle's followers are already accustomed to seeing snippets of her family life online—including her visits home to New Jersey—the Netflix series will offer much greater access to the people and places that have played an integral role in her life.

That includes the multimillion-dollar family mansion that has appeared repeatedly in her social media content and will now help set the scene as the Earles invite viewers further into their world than ever before.

The family appears to have made numerous upgrades to the dwelling in the six years since they bought it, with Earle's videos showcasing a much more modern and elegant interior than featured in the original listing images.

Meanwhile, records show that Earle's mother, Alisa, resides in a newly-built dwelling in nearby Point Pleasant.

When they are in New Jersey, the TikTok star and Ashtin, who resides in New York City, split their time between the two dwellings and it is understood that both parents will feature heavily in the Netflix series.

All episodes of “Earle Meets World” are scheduled to premiere on Netflix on Sept. 4.

In a previous press release announcing that Earle would be stepping into the world of reality TV, the TikTok star confessed that partnering with Netflix felt "unreal," adding that she was excited to show fans her life behind the scenes.

"It honestly feels unreal to be partnering with Netflix, and I’m so excited to be creating this show with them," she shared. "I’ve shared my life for years through my own camera, but this felt like the next phase because it’s a chance to go deeper.

"Not just the highlights, but the real moments, too. The vulnerable ones, the hard ones, and the fun, chaotic ones in between. It’s the same authenticity people know me for, but now with a different lens."

The social media mogul revealed that she was most "excited" for her fans to see her "fun" and "modern family."

"People either think we’re insane or they’re like, wait, this is exactly like my life. And honestly, both are true. I’m excited for fans to experience the full picture as it happens. The chaos, the emotional moments, the stressful parts, and all the little things in between that you don’t always see online," she added.

She admitted that the process was a "little scary," adding, "I’m so used to being in control of what I share and what I keep private, so having cameras around in moments I normally wouldn’t post is definitely an adjustment.

"But the real, human moments are what connected me to my audience in the first place. If letting people in even more makes someone feel less alone, or even just makes them laugh, then it’s worth it."
